title: Quiz: analytical evidence and reporting decisions
text:
Each answer should connect a number to its unit, sample basis and supporting evidence. A calculable candidate is not automatically a reportable chemical result.
Q1. A drink assay reports a peak area. State a suitable intended measurand for caffeine quantification.






Hint





Include analyte, material and quantity/unit rather than merely naming an instrument.









Answer





For example: caffeine mass concentration in the supplied drink, expressed in mg caffeine/L, under the defined preparation and sampling scope. Peak area is the response used to infer that quantity, not the measurand itself.




Q2. The calibration is area\(=4+40c\), valid over 0–30 mg/L final. An old sample reading gives 40 mg/L final. May you validate it just by editing the dilution factor?






Hint





Would that create a new response from a new prepared solution?









Answer





No. The measured solution was outside range. Prepare and measure an appropriate new dilution and record its actual aliquot and final volume. An edited factor does not add new measurement evidence.




Q3. A new accepted4.00 mL aliquot made to40.00 mL gives area 804. Calculate original concentration.






Hint





Invert the response model, then use40/4.









Answer





Final concentration is(804−4)/40=20 mg/L. The preparation factor is 10, giving200 mg/L original, conditional on the accepted identity, selectivity, QC and preparation evidence.




Q4. An unknown is within calibration range, but an independent check for its block recovers85% under a95–105% exercise rule. What should happen to the result?






Hint





Range and independent QC ask different questions.









Answer





Withhold the affected quantitative result and investigate/re-establish satisfactory calibration and checks before remeasurement. Being in range does not override failed QC. The failure alone does not prove a particular cause or justify dividing every value by 0.85.




Q5. The final estimate has standard uncertainty 0.20 mg/L and dilution factor 25. What is the dilution-scaled standard uncertainty on the original basis? Is it a 95% interval?






Hint





Propagate the supplied final estimate through the fixed scale factor; identify omitted inputs.









Answer





It is 0.20×25=5.0 mg/L under a fixed-factor model. It is a standard uncertainty, not automatically a 95% half-width. Actual dilution-volume, sampling, recovery and other omitted uncertainties would need evaluation for a full budget.




Q6. An ideal rounded calibration fits exactly. Does that establish zero uncertainty in real sample concentrations?






Hint





Which sources are absent from those ideal teaching points?









Answer





No. Real reading, standard preparation, volume, recovery and matrix effects can remain. Zero residual in deliberately idealised points is not a full uncertainty study; the final case supplies separate uncertainty inputs explicitly.




Q7. Two methods correlate extremely well, but one has increasing positive differences from a suitable reference. Are they interchangeable?






Hint





Association and agreement are different questions.









Answer





Not on correlation alone. Examine differences with reference uncertainty, sampling scope and the required analytical performance. A biased method can preserve rank and correlation while giving unsuitable amounts. The pattern motivates investigation rather than proving a chemical mechanism.




Q8. An ion near m/z195 is observed. Does that alone uniquely establish caffeine identity or its concentration?






Hint





Consider charge, protonation, fragments and calibration separately.









Answer





No. Singly protonated caffeine can appear near 195 even though its neutral nominal mass is 194, but other ions can share nominal mass. Suitable retention, standards, ion/fragment information and blanks can strengthen identity. Quantification separately requires an appropriate calibrated response and sample-preparation model.

title: Exercise: choose and defend an analytical result
text:
Background
For the independent final case, area \(=4+40c\) over 0–30 mg/L caffeine in the final solution. A separate check contains 15.00 mg/L and has area 608. The supplied check window is 95–105% recovery. Original concentration is final concentration times final/aliquot volume. The dataset supplies separation and sample-block QC decisions, and standard uncertainties of final concentration.
Those uncertainties are separate inputs: the rounded ideal calibration points’ zero residual does not imply zero real uncertainty. Scaling them by dilution excludes volume, sampling and recovery uncertainty. Molecular identity also requires suitable selective evidence; a matching retention time or nominal ion mass alone is not unique proof.

title: Exercise: choose and defend an analytical result
text:
By hand
B1. C1 has area 604 from5.00 mL made to50.00 mL. Separation and QC are accepted. Its supplied final standard uncertainty is 0.15 mg/L. Calculate final and original concentration and the dilution-scaled standard uncertainty. What does that uncertainty omit? Hint
B2. C2 of drink B has area 1604 from5.00 mL to50.00 mL. C3 is a newly prepared 2.00 mL aliquot of the same drink to50.00 mL, giving area 644. Calculate both candidates, choose what can be reported, and explain why C3 does not make C2’s old measurement valid. Hint
B3. C4’s area 484 lies within range and QC passes, but its candidate peak is unresolved. Can you report its algebraic caffeine concentration? What action would provide relevant new evidence? Hint
B4. A different instrument method gives a very high correlation with reference concentrations but increasingly positive differences. Does that establish acceptable agreement? Name the additional quantity or evidence you would examine. Hint

title: Exercise: choose and defend an analytical result
text:
Explore
The embedded experiment keeps an old signal fixed while you plan a different aliquot or measurement condition. The new-measurement button creates a new record. Its model is intentionally idealised; the exploratory case uses the same final standard uncertainty 0.15 mg/L for each accepted new preparation, whereas the separate archived C3 dataset supplies0.16 mg/L.



E1. The initial drink B record is outside range. Select a2.00 mL aliquot without measuring. What changes? Now click Measure a new preparation and compare old and new records. Connect the result to B2.
E2. Plan drink A at 5.00 mL with failed independent QC, then measure. Its candidate may remain in range: which gate stops reporting? Next choose an unresolved separation and accepted QC for a new preparation. Explain why changing one evidence condition does not erase failures in earlier records.
E3. Export the history. Which columns are diagnostic candidates, and which are actual reportable outputs? Why should a withheld concentration export as missing rather than zero? Reset and explain which teaching state resets.






Solutions — E1–E3





E1. Selecting a new plan alone changes no recorded area, volume or decision. The old B record remains area 1604, final candidate40 mg/L and withheld. The new 2.00 mL measurement gives area 644, final 16 mg/L and original 400 mg/L. In this demo its limited standard uncertainty is 0.15×25=3.75 mg/L; archived C3 separately has 0.16×25=4.0 mg/L. They are two stated uncertainty-input scenarios, not a contradiction or a complete method budget.
E2. The new failed-QC record is withheld even if its final candidate is in range. A later unresolved record is withheld for selectivity. Controls represent supplied new evidence under a new scenario; they are not a licence to relabel an old failed measurement. Record histories retain those distinctions.
E3. candidate_final_mg_l and candidate_original_mg_l are algebraic values used diagnostically. reported_original_mg_l and its limited uncertainty are empty for withheld records. Empty means unsupported, not zero caffeine. Reset returns the teaching model to its initial plan and history; it does not model deleting a real laboratory audit trail.

title: Exercise: choose and defend an analytical result
text:
Hints






Hint — B1





Invert area 4+40c, then multiply both concentration and the supplied final standard uncertainty by the dilution factor. Do not call a standard uncertainty a 95% half-width.









Hint — B2





Apply the range to the final measured solution, before any original-sample back-calculation. A new aliquot requires its own measurement and record.









Hint — B3





The response model assumes the integrated area belongs to caffeine. Known coelution challenges that interpretation even with a perfect calibration line.









Hint — B4





Correlation measures association. Differences on the concentration scale expose bias relative to the comparison reference, with its uncertainty and scope.









Hint — R1





Use lm() with area as response. case_when() can attach a decision while if_else() protects concentration fields from being exported as unsupported results.









Hint — R2





The same sample_id has a reference and both method results. Subtract reference from each matched method result, then plot difference against reference concentration.









Hint — R3





NA describes an absent estimate, not a concentration of zero. A singly protonated ion near m/z195 can support a caffeine investigation but is not by itself a unique identity or quantitative calibration.

title: Exercise: choose and defend an analytical result
text:
Solutions






Solutions — B1–B4





B1. \((604-4)/40=15\) mg/L final; factor 50/5=10 gives 150 mg/L original. The scaled standard uncertainty is 0.15×10=1.5 mg/L. It excludes volume, sampling, preparation recovery and other sources not in the supplied final estimate. It is not a 95% interval.
B2. C2 gives 40 mg/L final, outside the 0–30 mg/L working range. Its candidate original value 400 mg/L is not reportable. New C3 gives 16 mg/L final and factor 25, therefore400 mg/L original under accepted evidence. The equality of algebraic original values does not validate the old out-of-range signal.
B3. No: area 484 algebraically suggests12 mg/L final and 120 original, but known unresolved response makes that caffeine attribution unsupported. Improve separation or obtain justified additional selective evidence, then measure again.
B4. No. Plot method-minus-reference differences, evaluate reference uncertainty, sampling scope and the required performance. A systematic increasing discrepancy can coexist with extremely high correlation; the plot motivates investigation but does not prove the chemical cause.









Full worked R solutions — R1–R3





R1.
fit <- lm(area ~ caffeine_mg_l, data = standards)
a <- unname(coef(fit)[1])
b <- unname(coef(fit)[2])
qc <- qc |>
  mutate(estimated_mg_l = (area - a) / b,
         recovery_percent = 100 * estimated_mg_l / reference_mg_l,
         pass = recovery_percent >= acceptance_low &
                recovery_percent <= acceptance_high)
results <- samples |>
  mutate(candidate_final_mg_l = (area - a) / b,
         in_range = candidate_final_mg_l >= 0 & candidate_final_mg_l <= 30,
         reportable = in_range & resolved & qc_pass & all(qc$pass),
         dilution_factor = final_ml / aliquot_ml,
         original_mg_l = if_else(reportable,
                                candidate_final_mg_l * dilution_factor, NA_real_),
         u_original_mg_l = if_else(reportable,
           u_final_concentration_mg_l * dilution_factor, NA_real_),
         decision = case_when(!qc_pass | !all(qc$pass) ~ "withhold: QC",
                              !resolved ~ "withhold: coelution",
                              !in_range ~ "remeasure: outside range",
                              TRUE ~ "conditional result"))
qc
results |> select(preparation_id, sample_id, original_mg_l, u_original_mg_l, decision)
write_csv(results, "output/final-case-decisions.csv", na = "NA")
QC is 15.1 mg/L, or100.667% recovery, and passes. C1 and C3 report150 and 400 mg/L with limited standard uncertainties 1.5 and 4.0. C2 is outside range; C4 coelutes. Their reported concentrations and uncertainty fields are NA. Candidate fields remain diagnostic and must not be mistaken for reported measurements.
R2.
comparison <- read_csv("data/course/method-comparison.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
differences <- bind_rows(
  comparison |> transmute(sample_id, reference_mg_l,
    difference_mg_l = hplc_mg_l - reference_mg_l, method = "HPLC"),
  comparison |> transmute(sample_id, reference_mg_l,
    difference_mg_l = nonspecific_uv_mg_l - reference_mg_l, method = "Unseparated UV"))
ggplot(differences, aes(reference_mg_l, difference_mg_l, colour = method)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") + geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Reference result (mg/L)", y = "Method minus reference (mg/L)") +
  theme_minimal()
HPLC differs by 1–3 mg/L; unseparated UV differs by 13–45 mg/L with an increasing pattern. That suggests the latter method needs investigation for the intended use. The pattern does not itself identify a matrix mechanism or establish the reference as exact.
R3. A suitable conclusion reports conditional150 mg/L for A and 400 mg/L for B, with the stated limited uncertainties. C3 supplies B’s valid remeasurement; C2 remains outside range. C needs selective evidence and a new measurement. A peer should rebuild the report from saved inputs in a fresh R session.
# Optional: only after saving the exported history in data/.
if (file.exists("data/reporting-decisions.csv")) {
  history <- read_csv("data/reporting-decisions.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
  history |> select(preparation_id, recorded_area, reportable,
                     reported_original_mg_l, withheld_reason)
  stopifnot(all(is.na(history$reported_original_mg_l[!history$reportable])))
}
Identity and amount require related but distinct evidence. For example, a singly protonated caffeine ion near m/z195 differs from its nominal neutral mass 194. Adducts, charge states and fragments require interpretation; the course spectrum is illustrative, not an authentic library match. The MS signal would also need a suitable calibration for quantification.

text:
Where this leads
Carry the same traceability and withholding discipline into later laboratory reports. Choose a new measurement that resolves the actual uncertainty or selectivity problem rather than producing more digits from an unsupported model.

title: GC and HPLC
text:
About this lecture
Choose how an analyte can enter and move through a column.
Then ask which sources of variation an internal standard can actually track.

Retrieve separation principles before instrument names. The worked caffeine case is simulated and conditional on its supplied separation and QC evidence. We retain the introcomputing vocabulary: CSV import, mutate, lm, labelled plots.

title: GC and HPLC
text:
Follow the GC sample
Carrier gas → inlet → column in an oven → detector.


Conventional GC requires analyte entry into the gas phase and acceptable stability under introduction and separation conditions. Inlet and oven conditions are part of the method, not just hardware details. The drawing is schematic.

title: GC and HPLC
text:
Volatility concerns what is introduced
Headspace sampling can introduce volatiles above a nonvolatile matrix.
Retention depends on stationary-phase interactions as well as volatility.


The entire original sample need not be volatile. A headspace result depends on sampling partition and conditions. Temperature programming changes retention during a run, but retention order is not a universal boiling-point list.

title: GC and HPLC
text:
Follow the HPLC sample
Solvent reservoirs → controlled flow and injection → packed column → detector.


HPLC accommodates many compounds not suited to ordinary GC, provided solubility, stability and interactions suit the selected conditions. High pressure moves the liquid through the packed bed; it does not by itself create chemical selectivity.

title: GC and HPLC
section: Reversed phase is an interaction regime
text:
Reversed phase is an interaction regime
A relatively nonpolar stationary phase meets a more polar mobile phase.
Increasing organic modifier often reduces retention for appropriately retained compounds.


State the qualification. Ionisation and solvent/analyte chemistry can alter behaviour. Do not use a one-sentence rule as a method-development algorithm.

title: GC and HPLC
section: A gradient must include the next starting state
text:
A gradient must include the next starting state
Composition changes during a gradient; an isocratic run holds it fixed.
Return and re-equilibrate before the next injection.


The plotted program is illustrative, not a validated caffeine procedure. Its late return to ten percent organic supports repeating the initial conditions. Flow, column, temperature, solvent and injection settings also belong to the method.

title: GC and HPLC
text:
Detection adds another selectivity condition
UV absorption, flame-ionisation current and mass-to-charge signals are different responses.


A UV detector requires absorption at the selected wavelength. FID is useful for many organics in GC; MS detects ions. Their areas have method-specific response factors, so an area is not a universal number of molecules.

title: GC and HPLC
text:
Calibrate integrated caffeine area
Final-solution standards span 0–40 mg/L.
Area = 3 + 50 × caffeine concentration.


The supplied areas come from integration under assumed appropriate baseline and resolution. We fit area as response to known final concentration and retain the intercept. The result is not yet original drink concentration.

title: GC and HPLC
section: A smaller injection need not mean a weaker vial
text:
A smaller injection need not mean a weaker vial
Two injections of D1 give external estimates 15.00 and 12.00 mg/L final.


The same prepared solution is injected twice. Changes in introduced amount can change area while vial concentration remains unchanged. They are repeated injections, not independently collected drinks.

title: GC and HPLC
text:
Add a distinguishable internal standard
Every final standard and sample here has 10 mg/L internal standard.
Both peaks must be appropriately resolved.


The standard should follow the sources of variation it is intended to compensate. It must also be distinguishable from native matrix components. Addition timing is central to which losses it experiences.

title: GC and HPLC
text:
Calibrate the matched ratio
R=A_{caffeine}/A_{IS}=0.006+0.100c.


With constant IS concentration, ratio versus analyte concentration is appropriate for this example. If IS concentration varies, a concentration-ratio model is required. A ratio alone has no universal concentration unit.

title: GC and HPLC
text:
Compare the repeated-injection estimates
Ratio estimates: 15.000 and 15.015 mg/L final.
The common injection effect mostly cancels.


The retained constant analyte offset prevents perfect cancellation: it does not scale with the injection factor. Keep this small residual distinct from an unshared matrix or extraction effect.

title: GC and HPLC
text:
Return to the original drink
The preparation factor is 10, giving about 150 mg caffeine/L original.


Invert the fitted ratio first, then multiply by the correct preparation factor. Do not apply an extra factor because the internal standard itself has a concentration. The fixed-standard calibration already includes that design.

title: GC and HPLC
section: Timing determines which loss is tracked
text:
Timing determines which loss is tracked
A standard added after extraction cannot establish recovery of native analyte through that extraction.


Even an early freely added standard may differ from native bound analyte. Equivalent behaviour is an assumption requiring evidence. The embedded demo lets students compare timing under an explicit equal-recovery idealisation.

title: GC and HPLC
text:
Ratios cannot restore missing selectivity
I3 is unresolved. I4 has failed QC.
Both concentration results are withheld despite calculable areas and ratios.


The flags in the exercise are supplied outcomes of separation and QC review, not switches chosen to retain a desired answer. An interfering peak can contaminate either analyte or standard area.

title: GC and HPLC
text:
Encode the chemical decision
reportable <- resolved & qc_pass & in_range


A reproducible decision should preserve IDs, preparation factors and reasons. A missing withheld estimate is not zero analyte. Do not manufacture a complete uncertainty from the few repeat injections provided.

title: GC and HPLC
text:
Predict before exploring
Change only injection amount. Then introduce a loss that occurs before a late internal standard.
Which error cancels, and which remains?


Use the embedded exercise experiment. Shared injection gives nearly constant ratio estimates. A late standard cannot cancel earlier analyte recovery loss, and differential analyte response does not cancel either.

title: GC and HPLC
text:
Transfer the calibrated ratio
Areas 903 and 600; same IS concentration; original-to-final factor 5.
What amount would you report, and what could still prevent reporting?


Ratio1.505; final 14.99 mg/L; original 74.95 mg/L. If a known unresolved absorber contributes, withhold the simple caffeine interpretation. The same equation cannot fix the selectivity failure.

title: GC and HPLC
text:
Choose the complete method
Volatile solvent mixture versus heat-sensitive nonvolatile solutes.
Exercise and embedded exploration · Practice quiz


GC is a plausible starting point for the volatile solvent mixture and LC for the heat-sensitive nonvolatile solutes. Matrix, sample entry, detector, selectivity and uncertainty requirements refine the choice. Read Harris and Lucy by GC/HPLC topic.

title: Quiz: retention, resolution and selective areas
text:
Try each question before opening its independent hint or answer. Use the stated width definition and explain the chemical interpretation, not only the arithmetic.
Q1. An unretained marker takes0.50 min and an analyte peak takes1.50 min. What is its retention factor?






Hint





Retention factor describes delay beyond unretained transit: \(k=(t_R-t_0)/t_0\).









Answer





\(k=(1.50-0.50)/0.50=2.00\). Dividing1.50 by 0.50 without subtracting transit would give 3 and the wrong definition.




Q2. Peaks are at 4.00 and 4.60 min, with baseline widths 0.40 and 0.80 min. Calculate resolution.






Hint





Use \(R_s=2\Delta t_R/(w_1+w_2)\), keeping all time units the same.









Answer





\(R_s=2(0.60)/(0.40+0.80)=1.00\). It is dimensionless. The value describes spacing relative to these baseline widths; it does not by itself prove purity or quantify the integration error.




Q3. The export contains half-height widths rather than baseline widths. Can you use the same coefficient2 in the preceding formula?






Hint





Width definitions are part of the formula, not interchangeable labels.









Answer





No. A half-height-width resolution formula needs its appropriate coefficient. Substituting another width definition unchanged changes the numerical meaning of the result.




Q4. An ideal Gaussian peak doubles in width at fixed area and retention time. What happens to height? If both peaks double their widths, what happens to their resolution?






Hint





Area is proportional to Gaussian height times width; the resolution numerator remains fixed.









Answer





The height halves and full area stays fixed. Doubling both widths doubles the resolution denominator and therefore halves resolution. Mean retention factors and relative selectivity stay unchanged.




Q5. Two separations have the same retention times and widths, but the second has a much larger neighbouring component. Must the integrated area assigned to A have the same relative contamination?






Hint





Does resolution include peak amount?









Answer





No. Resolution depends on times and widths, not relative component area. A larger neighbouring contribution can create more contamination in A’s integration window at the same resolution. Adequacy depends on the quantitative task.




Q6. A peak occurs at an authentic standard’s expected retention time and has no visible shoulder. Does that uniquely identify it?






Hint





Could another component arrive at the same time?









Answer





No. Matching retention under controlled conditions supports identity but does not exclude coelution. Appropriate standards, separation review or additional selective evidence can strengthen the assignment. An apparently single peak is not proof of a single compound.




Q7. A CSV has 1401 time positions for one run. Are there1401 independent samples?






Hint





Identify what one row represents.









Answer





No. They are dependent measurement positions in a within-run time series. Independent sample, preparation and injection counts come from the experimental design and identifiers, not the number of trace rows.

title: Exercise: retention, resolution and peak area
text:
Background
Chromatography delays solutes through interaction with a stationary phase while a mobile phase carries them along. A chromatogram records detector response over time at the outlet, not position inside the column.







Quantity
Definition in this exercise




Unretained transit time
\(t_0\)


Retention factor
\(k=(t_R-t_0)/t_0\)


Relative selectivity, B later than A
\(\alpha=k_B/k_A\)


Resolution using baseline widths
\(R_s=2(t_{RB}-t_{RA})/(w_A+w_B)\)


Gaussian width in the demo
\(w_b=4\sigma\)


Area
Integrated response above the stated baseline; requires calibration for amount



IUPAC retention factor and peak resolution define the terminology. A numerical resolution is not proof of purity. Peak shape, relative amount, detector selectivity and the required accuracy also matter.

title: Exercise: retention, resolution and peak area
text:
By hand
B1. A has \(t_R=3.00\) min and baseline width 0.40 min. B has \(t_R=4.00\) min and width 0.50 min. The unretained marker is at 1.00 min. Calculate both retention factors, selectivity and resolution. Hint
B2. Keep retention times and full areas fixed, but double both widths. Calculate the new resolution. For ideal Gaussian peaks, what happens to height and full integrated area? Hint
B3. An integration window captures 95.45 response·min from A and 20.00 from B. A’s full area is 100.00. Calculate the combined window area and B’s fraction of it. Why is assigning the combined area to A unjustified? Hint
B4. For a new pair, \(t_0=0.80\) min, retention times are 2.40 and 3.20 min, and baseline widths are 0.40 and 0.60 min. Calculate \(k_A,k_B,\alpha,R_s\). Would the same formula accept half-height widths? Hint

title: Exercise: retention, resolution and peak area
text:
Explore
Predict each change before touching the controls. Curves are ideal Gaussian components with known simulation areas; the combined response is what a nonselective detector would see. The finite window around A spans ±2σ, so it captures about 95.45% of isolated A plus any B inside it.



E1. Check B1 at the defaults. Set the width multiplier to 2 without changing spacing or B area. Which numbers change, and which remain fixed?
E2. Reset, set the spacing to 0.25 min and compare B areas 150 and 500. Does resolution change? Does B’s fraction of A’s window change? Explain why a single resolution threshold cannot establish an acceptable quantitative result.
E3. Hide the individual components. Could the combined curve alone tell you the true separate areas without a justified model or additional evidence? Export the CSV for R3, then explain what its component columns represent.






Solutions — E1–E3





E1. Default \(k_A=2\), \(k_B=3\), \(\alpha=1.5\) and \(R_s=2.222\). Doubling widths halves resolution to 1.111. The full areas remain 100 and 150; each Gaussian height halves. A’s ±2σ window broadens, so a neighbour can contribute more to it.
E2. At spacing 0.25 min the resolution is \(2(0.25)/0.90=0.5556\) for both amounts. Increasing B’s area increases its contamination of the A window without changing the retention times or widths. Therefore equal resolution can accompany different quantitative errors. A value alone is not a purity or acceptance test.
E3. No. A combined response can be consistent with more than one allocation of component areas. The exported component_a and component_b columns reveal the simulation’s construction; real data do not automatically supply them. A model-based deconvolution would need its own assumptions and validation.

title: Exercise: retention, resolution and peak area
text:
Hints






Hint — B1 and B4





Subtract \(t_0\) before dividing by it. Resolution uses the difference in retention times and the sum of the stated baseline widths. All time units cancel.









Hint — B2





The numerator of resolution stays fixed while its denominator doubles. A Gaussian has area proportional to height times width.









Hint — B3





The detector records both contributions. Divide B’s contribution by the combined window area, not by A’s full area, for the requested fraction.









Hint — R1





Use mutate(), then group_by(run) and summarise(). Expressions such as k[compound == "A"] identify a component within each supplied two-component run.









Hint — R2





Plot response against time_min, mapping colour = run. A time position is part of a dependent within-run series, not another collected sample.









Hint — R3





For ordered times, sum \(\Delta t_i(y_i+y_{i+1})/2\) after subtracting the baseline. diff() returns successive differences; head(x,-1) and tail(x,-1) pair neighbours.

title: Exercise: retention, resolution and peak area
text:
Solutions






Solutions — B1–B4





B1. \(k_A=(3-1)/1=2\), \(k_B=(4-1)/1=3\), \(\alpha=3/2=1.5\), \(R_s=2(4-3)/(0.40+0.50)=2.222\). Using \(t_R/t_0\) alone would incorrectly include the unretained transit contribution in the retention factor.
B2. \(R_s=2/1.80=1.111\). At fixed Gaussian area, doubling width halves height. The full area is unchanged. A finite integration window is a different quantity: it can exclude some A and include some B.
B3. Combined window area is 115.45 response·min. B contributes \(20/115.45\times 100=17.32\%\). Assigning all 115.45 to A both includes B and misses part of A outside the window; it is not a selective measurement of A’s amount.
B4. \(k_A=2\), \(k_B=3\), \(\alpha=1.5\), \(R_s=2(0.80)/(0.40+0.60)=1.60\). Half-height widths require their corresponding formula/coefficient; they cannot be substituted into this baseline-width formula unchanged.









Full worked R solutions — R1–R3





R1. Preserve component and run identities:
peaks <- peaks |> mutate(k = (t_r_min - t0_min) / t0_min)
resolution <- peaks |>
  group_by(run) |>
  summarise(k_A = k[compound == "A"], k_B = k[compound == "B"],
            alpha = k_B / k_A,
            resolution = 2 * (t_r_min[compound == "B"] -
                              t_r_min[compound == "A"]) /
                          sum(baseline_width_min), .groups = "drop")
resolution
write_csv(resolution, "output/separation-resolution.csv")
Resolved, overlap and broad runs give resolution 2.2222, 0.6667 and 0.9091. The broad and resolved runs have the same \(k_A=2,k_B=3,\alpha=1.5\); overlap changes \(k_B\) to 2.3 and \(\alpha\) to 1.15.
R2.
ggplot(chrom, aes(time_min, response, colour = run)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Time (min)", y = "Detector response", colour = "Run") +
  theme_minimal()
Overlap changes retention spacing. Broad changes widths at unchanged retention times. Each line is a within-run trace: time positions do not represent repeated independent sampling of the original material.
R3. The data are already ordered by time within run:
area_summary <- chrom |>
  group_by(run) |>
  summarise(total_area = sum(diff(time_min) *
             (head(response - 5, -1) + tail(response - 5, -1)) / 2),
            .groups = "drop")
area_summary
write_csv(area_summary, "output/separation-areas.csv")
Every total is about 250 response·min, because component areas remain 100+150. That conservation does not establish a unique allocation from the combined signal. For the optional saved demo file, put the download in data/:
# Optional: only after saving this exported file in data/.
if (file.exists("data/separation-experiment.csv")) {
  demo <- read_csv("data/separation-experiment.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
  area_a <- sum(diff(demo$time_min) *
    (head(demo$component_a, -1) + tail(demo$component_a, -1)) / 2)
  area_b <- sum(diff(demo$time_min) *
    (head(demo$component_b, -1) + tail(demo$component_b, -1)) / 2)
  c(area_a = area_a, area_b = area_b)
}
Those two columns are known model contributions. A real mixed trace does not supply them without additional modelling or selective evidence.

title: Atomic measurements
text:
About this lecture

Distinguish atomic absorption from optical emission.
Inspect spectral overlap and independent quality checks.
Undo dilution and correct the method blank on a common basis before reporting dry mass.


The exercise begins with pen-and-paper tasks, then embeds the exploratory model and finishes in R using the existing course datasets. Keep each numerical result connected to its chemical quantity. All data and profiles are simulated; the demonstrations do not validate actual instruments or preparation methods.

title: Atomic measurements
text:
Which information survives atomisation?

An element amount can survive; original molecular identity generally does not.

A plant copper result is not evidence of the original copper-binding molecule or oxidation state.

title: Atomic measurements
text:
Absorption supplies the photon

A source photon promotes a suitable free atom to a higher state.

Energy must match an allowed transition. The relevant population depends on atomisation conditions.

title: Atomic measurements
text:
Emission releases the photon

An excited population emits characteristic light during transitions.

Excitation is supplied by the atomisation/excitation environment. Not every introduced atom contributes the same response regardless of matrix.

title: Atomic measurements
text:
Follow the AAS path

Element source → atomiser → selected wavelength → detector.

The detector compares transmitted source light. Do not describe flame emission alone as the AAS measured signal.

title: Atomic measurements
text:
The flame introduces material continuously

Transport and atomisation affect sensitivity.

The selected source/wavelength, sample introduction and matrix compatibility belong to the measurement method.

title: Atomic measurements
section: The graphite furnace treats a small aliquot
text:
The graphite furnace treats a small aliquot

A heating program separates drying, matrix removal and atomisation.

Small volume and high sensitivity are not guarantees against matrix effects. Discuss the different introduction strategy without an exhaustive furnace-design survey.

title: Atomic measurements
text:
Follow the ICP optical-emission path

Aerosol → plasma excitation → wavelength separation → detector.

This measures emitted light. It is not ICP-MS, which detects ions by mass-to-charge.

title: Atomic measurements
section: Many elements means many possible lines
text:
Many elements means many possible lines

Line choice and background still matter.

Multielement capability does not imply zero spectral overlap or zero matrix effects.

title: Atomic measurements
text:
Look around the target line

Which signal would a broad integration window include?

The illustrative neighbouring feature can bias the selected line measurement. These are simulated profiles, not reference identification spectra.

title: Atomic measurements
section: An interference need not look like a separate peak
text:
An interference need not look like a separate peak

Transport and chemical effects can change the target population.

A stable reading does not prove correct recovery. Alternative lines, matrix-matched checks and suitable validation can address different issues.

title: Atomic measurements
text:
Calibrate the introduced solution

Concentration axis: mg copper/L measured solution.

The solution is not yet on a dry-material basis. Fit counts as response and retain the intercept.

title: Atomic measurements
text:
Check with independent material

Both supplied checks meet the exercise 95–105% rule.

Recoveries are about 100.37 and 100.77 percent. They test the check solution conditions, not plant digestion completeness.

title: Atomic measurements
section: Trace the sample mass and volumes
text:
Trace the sample mass and volumes

A1: 0.2500 g dry material → 50.00 mL digest → twofold dilution.

No full recovery validation is supplied. Result is conditional on quantitative transfer and digestion under the scenario.

title: Atomic measurements
text:
Convert the sample signal

A1 measured solution ≈ 0.40189 mg/L copper.

The calibration response range is zero to two mg/L. Check introduced solution concentration before back-calculating.

title: Atomic measurements
section: The method blank has a different dilution history
text:
The method blank has a different dilution history

Blank digest is measured undiluted.

Its measured concentration is about 0.0019922 mg/L. The sample has a further factor of two, but the blank does not.

title: Atomic measurements
text:
Subtract on a common basis

A1 digest: 0.40189 × 2 − 0.001992 = 0.80179 mg/L.

First undo sample dilution, then subtract blank digest concentration. Multiplying a blank by a dilution it never underwent would be wrong.

title: Atomic measurements
section: Recover amount, then divide by original mass
text:
Recover amount, then divide by original mass

0.80179 mg/L × 0.05000 L / 0.0002500 kg = 160.36 mg/kg dry.

Ask students to cancel units. A concentration in digest and a mass fraction in original material are different quantities.

title: Atomic measurements
section: A blank has no sample mass denominator
text:
A blank has no sample mass denominator

No mg/kg plant result is assigned to the method blank.

Preserve its preparation role and report blank evidence without pretending it is a zero-mass sample concentration.

title: Atomic measurements
section: Passing a dissolved check cannot prove digestion recovery
text:
Passing a dissolved check cannot prove digestion recovery

What material would better challenge the whole preparation?

A suitable reference material and/or appropriate recovery study, with evidence that the measurand and matrix are relevant.

title: Atomic measurements
section: Uncertainty needs more than counting noise
text:
Uncertainty needs more than counting noise

Mass, volume, calibration, blank variation and recovery can all contribute.

The worked elemental result is a conditional point estimate. Do not invent a complete uncertainty from the few numbers given.

title: Atomic measurements
section: Choose among instruments for the question
text:
Choose among instruments for the question

Range, matrix, elements, sample volume, throughput and required uncertainty.

Avoid a universal ranking that declares one instrument best. Revisit flame, furnace and plasma differences.

title: Atomic measurements
section: Transfer the blank and dry-mass basis
text:
Transfer the blank and dry-mass basis

0.2000 g to 25.00 mL; fivefold dilution reads 0.0800 mg/L; blank digest 0.0100 mg/L.

Corrected digest is 0.3900 mg/L. Result is 48.75 mg/kg dry mass. Require the blank and dilution order.

title: Quiz: matrix effects and standard addition
text:
Try each question before opening its hint. Then explain the answer in chemical and measurement terms. Lecture · Exercise.

Q1. Why do the standard-addition flasks use equal sample aliquots and equal final volumes?






Hint





Track native concentration and matrix fraction.









Answer





Both remain constant across flasks, while added-analyte concentration varies. Changing final volume without correction would also change native concentration and matrix fraction, invalidating the simple fixed-volume intercept formula.




Q2. Matched unspiked/spiked final solutions give external estimates 2.00 and 2.80 mg/L after adding 1.00 mg/L. Calculate incremental recovery.






Hint





Use the change in the estimate, not the full spiked value.









Answer





Recovery is \(100(2.80-2.00)/1.00=\mathbf{80\%}\). It tests incremental response from the point of addition under the matched design, not automatically total native recovery.




Q3. Equal 4.00 mL sample aliquots made to 20.00 mL give \(y=0.360+0.120c_{added,final}\). What original concentration is inferred?






Hint





First find the negative x-intercept; then undo sample dilution.









Answer





\(x_0=-0.360/0.120=-3.00\) mg/L final. Its magnitude multiplied by \(20/4=5\) gives 15.0 mg/L original under the stated additive model. Negative concentration was not physically prepared.




Q4. An unrelated constant signal remains in every flask. Can an exact straight standard-addition line prove the native analyte estimate is correct?






Hint





What else contributes to the intercept?









Answer





No. A constant additive interference increases the intercept and is misread as native analyte. Shared multiplicative sensitivity cancels in intercept/slope, but an uncorrected additive term does not. Independent background/selectivity evidence is needed.




Q5. A spike added after extraction recovers 100%. Can native analyte still have been lost during extraction?






Hint





Ask which steps the added material experienced.









Answer





Yes. The spike bypassed the earlier loss and tests only later behaviour. Even a pre-extraction freely dissolved spike may not mimic native bound analyte; the chemical equivalence assumption needs evidence.




Q6. Does an ordinary response confidence interval for the fitted intercept automatically give a confidence interval for original standard-addition concentration?






Hint





The target quantity is a ratio of coefficients times a volume ratio.









Answer





No. The target depends on intercept, slope, their covariance and preparation volumes. A forward response interval has another target; a suitable inverse uncertainty calculation and its assumptions are needed.

title: Exercise: matrix effects and standard addition
text:
Background
All signals in the supplied standard-addition data are already background corrected. Each flask contains the same 10.00 mL sample made to 25.00 mL total. Added-analyte concentration refers to this final volume. Under an additive linear model with shared native/spike sensitivity,
\[y=b\left(c_s\frac{V_s}{V_f}+c_{added,final}\right)=a+b c_{added,final}.\]
The negative x-intercept is \(x_0=-a/b\); its magnitude estimates native analyte in the diluted final flask, so \(c_s=-x_0V_f/V_s\). A constant unrelated signal also shifts the intercept unless independently corrected. A successful spike after extraction never passed through earlier native losses. The simulated course data are separate analytical scenarios, not a validation of a real assay.

title: Exercise: matrix effects and standard addition
text:
By hand
B1. Equal-final-volume unspiked/spiked solutions give external-calibration estimates 1.50 and 2.25 mg/L after adding 1.00 mg/L in the final flask. Calculate incremental recovery and state what those units refer to. Hint
B2. Equal 10.00 mL sample aliquots made to 25.00 mL give the fitted line \(y=0.3004+0.1496c_{added,final}\). Calculate x-intercept and original concentration. Why is zero added analyte not a zero-analyte blank? Hint
B3. A second design uses 5.00 mL sample made to 20.00 mL and gives \(y=0.240+0.120c_{added,final}\). Calculate the original concentration. Would the same formula work without adjustment if final volumes differed between flasks? Hint
B4. Native analyte loses half its amount before a freely dissolved spike is added. Native recovered and added material then give equal response. Can late-spike recovery be 100%? Would that establish native recovery? Hint

title: Exercise: matrix effects and standard addition
text:
Explore
Keep the original input visible as simulation truth. Change one mechanism at a time. The independent-background switch assumes a perfect independent estimate of the interfering term; standard addition itself does not supply it.



E1. With complete native recovery and no additive signal, set sensitivity ratio to 0.75. Compare external and standard-addition estimates. Explain which quantity changes with suppression. Hint
E2. Restore sensitivity ratio one, reduce native recovery to 50%, and keep additive signal zero. Explain why a perfect late-spike recovery can coexist with a wrong original amount. Hint
E3. Set sensitivity ratio back to 0.75, restore native recovery, add an interference of 0.120 signal units, and examine the exact straight line. Then apply the ideal independent correction. Explain what changed and what extra evidence was assumed. Export one scenario. Hint

title: Exercise: matrix effects and standard addition
text:
In R
Run this workflow at the project root in a fresh R session. Use standard-addition and external standards in their correct separate tables.
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
additions <- read_csv("data/course/standard-addition.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
external <- read_csv("data/course/external-matrix.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
fit_sa <- lm(blank_corrected_signal ~ spike_mg_l_final, data = additions)
fit_ext <- lm(blank_corrected_signal ~ c_mg_l, data = external)
a_sa <- unname(coef(fit_sa)[1]); b_sa <- unname(coef(fit_sa)[2])
x_intercept <- -a_sa / b_sa
original_sa_mg_l <- -x_intercept * 25.00 / 10.00
original_external_mg_l <- unname(
  (additions$blank_corrected_signal[1] - coef(fit_ext)[1]) / coef(fit_ext)[2]) * 25 / 10
line <- data.frame(spike_mg_l_final = seq(-2.3, 2.2, length.out = 100)) |>
  mutate(blank_corrected_signal = a_sa + b_sa * spike_mg_l_final)
ggplot(additions, aes(spike_mg_l_final, blank_corrected_signal)) +
  geom_point() + geom_line(data = line) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Added analyte in final flask (mg/L)", y = "Background-corrected signal") +
  theme_minimal()
spikes <- read_csv("data/course/spike-recovery.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
spike_recovery_percent <- 100 * diff(spikes$externally_estimated_mg_l_final) /
                               diff(spikes$added_mg_l_final)
answers <- data.frame(standard_addition_mg_l = original_sa_mg_l,
                      external_mg_l = original_external_mg_l,
                      incremental_recovery_percent = spike_recovery_percent)
answers
write_csv(answers, "output/matrix-recovery-exercise.csv")
R1. Read the x-intercept and volume correction with units. Explain why negative analyte is not physically prepared. Hint
R2. Compare the two fitted slopes and original concentration estimates. Explain why an external standard can be precisely prepared yet inappropriate for this sample. Hint
R3. Does the fitted intercept’s ordinary response interval automatically give an interval for original concentration? Identify the uncertain inputs and one assumption that could invalidate a straight-line standard-addition answer. Hint

title: Exercise: matrix effects and standard addition
text:
Hints






B1: use the increment, not the full spiked result





Subtract the unspiked estimate from the spiked estimate, then divide by the known added concentration on the same final-volume basis.









B2: first find the diluted native concentration





Solve \(0=a+b x_0\) and multiply its magnitude by \(25/10\). The unspiked sample already contains native analyte.









B3: the sample fraction is part of the model





Use \(V_f/V_s=4\). Different final volumes change both native concentration and matrix fraction across the series.









B4: trace the spike path





The added analyte was not present during the loss. It can test later response without testing earlier recovery.









E1: the shared slope cancels





The intercept and slope both scale under the same multiplicative effect; their ratio does not. An unrelated additive term behaves differently.









E2: recovered is not original





At five mg/L original and half native recovery, the later prepared material represents only 2.5 mg/L on the original-sample basis.









E3: a line does not identify its intercept components





The intercept contains native response plus the additive term. Removing the latter requires evidence beyond merely fitting additions.









R1: model-based extrapolation





The negative x-axis position is inferred from the additive response model. It is not an ordinary unknown measured beyond its external calibration.









R2: compare sensitivities





Read coef for each model. A slope difference changes the response per concentration even with an apparently excellent fit.









R3: propagate through the ratio





Original concentration uses intercept divided by slope and a volume ratio. Their covariance and volume uncertainties matter; a forward response interval has a different target.

title: Exercise: matrix effects and standard addition
text:
Solutions






Full worked solutions





B1. Increment is \(2.25-1.50=0.75\) mg/L. Divide by the added 1.00 mg/L and multiply by 100 to obtain 75%. Both concentrations refer to final solutions with equal total volume and sample fraction, so the difference isolates an increment under the stated matched design.
B2. \(x_0=-0.3004/0.1496=-2.0080214\) mg/L final. Original concentration is \(2.0080214\times25/10=\mathbf{5.0200535}\) mg/L. An aliquot with no added standard still contains the sample’s native analyte, so it is not a zero-analyte blank.
B3. \(x_0=-2.00\) mg/L final; multiply by four to get 8.00 mg/L original. Different final volumes require an appropriate volume-corrected model. The fixed-volume intercept formula cannot be reused as though the matrix fraction and native concentration were constant.
B4. Yes: added material can respond quantitatively after the loss, giving 100% incremental recovery. It did not experience the loss and cannot establish native recovery. A successful post-extraction spike is not a mass balance for the original material.
E1. At default five mg/L original, standard addition returns 5.000 mg/L while external calibration returns 3.750 mg/L in the exact demo model. The sensitivity is suppressed from 0.200 to 0.150. Shared scaling cancels in intercept/slope, but external calibration uses the wrong slope.
E2. At ratio one and 50% native recovery, standard addition returns 2.500 mg/L, yet late-spike recovery is 100%. All later response is correct; the input already lost analyte. No calibration can reconstruct that loss without additional recovery evidence.
E3. With ratio 0.75, complete recovery and additive signal 0.120, the intercept increases and the standard-addition estimate becomes 7.000 mg/L although the native truth is 5.000. Perfect independent subtraction returns it to 5.000. This assumes the interferent was separately established under relevant conditions; a reagent blank need not reveal a sample-specific signal. Exact linearity did not distinguish the two intercept contributions.
R1. The supplied noisy teaching data give 5.02005 mg/L original via the negative final-flask intercept −2.00802 mg/L. Negative concentration is not prepared; its location follows from the specified additive response model with fixed sample fraction, not a licence to extrapolate every calibration.
R2. External slope is 0.1998, matrix slope 0.1496 signal units per mg/L. The external estimate is 3.76126 mg/L original, lower than the standard-addition estimate. Standard preparation precision cannot establish sample matrix compatibility. The separate spike data give 75% incremental recovery.
R3. No. The inferred quantity depends on \(a/b\) and \(V_f/V_s\), so uncertainty in both coefficients (including covariance) and volumes must be propagated. A forward response interval for \(a\) is not an inverse original-concentration interval. Nonlinear response, changing sample fraction, residual additive interference or different native/spike behaviour can invalidate the model. This exercise therefore reports a conditional point estimate, not a complete uncertainty interval.

title: UV and visible absorption
text:
About this lecture
A coloured solution gives an absorbance. We want mg elemental Fe/L in the supplied filtered water.

Explain what absorbs and how light is measured.
Fit a justified calibration and return to the original sample basis.
Decide what range, QC and uncertainty evidence permit us to report.


Retrieve the straight-line calibration from introcomputing. The chemical absorber and preparation now matter: students must connect the response to the intended measurand. All data are simulated. The exercise includes by-hand calculations before R.

title: UV and visible absorption
text:
The chemical absorber
Iron is reduced to Fe(II), then complexed with excess 1,10-phenanthroline (phen).
We assume quantitative conversion and no analyte loss.


Three bidentate ligands bind one iron ion. The diagram shows stoichiometry, not molecular geometry. The result after reduction is not the original Fe(II) fraction. Ask what incomplete reduction would do: it can bias the inferred amount low. Background: https://staff.buffalostate.edu/nazareay/che301/l9.pdf .

title: UV and visible absorption
text:
What the detector measures
T=I/I_0, then A=-\log_{10}T.
A reagent blank establishes the reference under matched conditions.


Distinguish source/reference intensity from transmitted light. These supplied absorbances are already reagent-blank referenced. Another subtraction would change their basis. A whole-procedure method blank can answer a different contamination question.

title: UV and visible absorption
text:
Why select a wavelength?
A strong response near 510 nm supports useful sensitivity.
A maximum does not prove the sample has no other absorber.


The spectral envelope is a simulated Gaussian illustration, not a reference spectrum for identification. A maximum also makes small wavelength errors less consequential than a steep flank. Wavelength positions within a scan are not independent samples.

title: UV and visible absorption
text:
Beer–Lambert connects light and composition
A=\varepsilon l c at fixed wavelength, with appropriate chemical and instrumental conditions.
For a molar absorptivity, c is in mol/L. Our empirical line instead uses mg Fe/L.

Explain why concentration basis matters. A fitted slope in L/mg Fe is not numerically a molar absorptivity. Fixed path and chemical state matter; stray light and chemical changes can break the relation. Give the exercise tiny calculation A=.6 at epsilon2000 and path1 -> c=.0003 mol/L.

title: UV and visible absorption
section: Doubling absorbance does not halve transmission
text:
Doubling absorbance does not halve transmission
T=0.80\Rightarrow A\approx0.09691.
If A doubles, T=10^{-A} becomes 0.64, not 0.40.


Ask students to predict first. Squaring 0.80 gives 0.64, clearly different from halving to 0.40. The special case T=0.50 would square to 0.25 and happen to equal halving, so it cannot by itself demonstrate the general distinction. The logarithm is why proportional absorbance corresponds to exponential attenuation; B1 compares both starting values.

title: UV and visible absorption
section: Fit the quantity we deliberately varied
text:
Fit the quantity we deliberately varied
Known final concentrations are the explanatory variable; absorbance is the response.
fit <- lm(absorbance ~ standard_mg_l, data = standards)


Eighteen independent prepared standard solutions span zero to four mg Fe/L final, each measured once. Reversing the regression is a different least-squares problem. Retain the fitted intercept rather than forcing zero.

title: UV and visible absorption
text:
Interpret the fitted relationship
A=0.003874+0.198799c_{final}.
The slope has units L/mg Fe; the offset is estimated from the data.


Use full precision in code and rounded values in prose. The nonzero offset does not identify its cause. Concentration zero does not guarantee an exactly zero observed reading. Highlight one known standard and ask for its expected response.

title: UV and visible absorption
section: Residuals ask whether the line misses structure
text:
Residuals ask whether the line misses structure
Residual = observed response − fitted response.
Inspect curvature, changing spread and unusual points before accepting the model.


A high R squared alone is insufficient. Small residuals here support the selected simple model, but do not establish recovery in an unknown matrix. Do not remove an inconvenient standard just to improve appearance.

title: UV and visible absorption
text:
Invert the response model
\hat c_{final}=(\overline A-a)/b.
P01 has \overline A=0.480620, giving 2.398 mg Fe/L final.

The inverse is algebraically simple but uncertain slope and intercept also contribute to its uncertainty. This remains final-solution concentration. Ask what additional record is required before reporting the original water concentration.

title: UV and visible absorption
text:
Count the experimental units
P01 and P02 are separate preparations of W1; each has three readings.
Six readings are not six independently collected waters.


Readings describe instrument repeatability within a solution. Separate preparations probe additional variation. Both preparations share a calibration and original collected sample, so their uncertainty components are not all independent.

title: UV and visible absorption
section: Carry the preparation record into the calculation
text:
Carry the preparation record into the calculation
c_{original}=c_{final} V_{final}/V_{aliquot}.
P01: 2.398\times50.00/10.00\approx 11.99 mg Fe/L original.


The total final volume includes reagents and solvent. Distinguish making up to fifty millilitres from adding fifty millilitres. In R match preparation records by ID; table row order has no chemical meaning.

title: UV and visible absorption
section: A new dilution means a new measurement
text:
A new dilution means a new measurement
P03 exceeds the calibrated response range.
P04 is a new 5.00 mL aliquot made to 50.00 mL and measured again.


P03 mean absorbance is 1.07507, beyond range. Editing its dilution factor cannot fix that reading. P04 mean is .54061 and its factor is ten, giving about twenty-seven mg Fe/L original. Crosses in the figure locate signals diagnostically; unsupported concentrations remain withheld.

title: UV and visible absorption
section: Independent QC can block an in-range result
text:
Independent QC can block an in-range result
Check material: 2.00 mg Fe/L. Exercise acceptance: 95–105% recovery.
The later block B fails, so P05 is withheld.


A recovers99.6%, later B85.2%. Passing a calibration at the beginning does not establish later performance. Investigate, correct, re-establish satisfactory checks and remeasure. Do not automatically divide samples by the failed QC ratio. The chosen window is an exercise rule, not universal validation.

title: UV and visible absorption
text:
Uncertainty survives repeat readings
P01: 11.991 mg Fe/L, with standard uncertainty 0.028 mg Fe/L from the stated model.
That number is not a 95% half-width.


The supplied helper includes reading noise and full slope/intercept covariance in an inverse first-order approximation. Independent volume components are added in quadrature. Sampling, recovery, matrix bias and standard concentration uncertainty are omitted. The limited budget is not full method validation.

title: UV and visible absorption
section: A result needs its chemical assumptions
text:
A result needs its chemical assumptions
Which check addresses contamination? Which challenges the line? Which could detect a sample-specific matrix effect?


Return to reagent/method blanks, independent check material and sample spikes. No one check answers all three questions. Have students identify a missing source before calling a result fit for purpose.

title: UV and visible absorption
section: Explore the mechanism, then test a claim
text:
Explore the mechanism, then test a claim
Embedded experiment: change path or wavelength, then introduce stray light.
Predict the response before moving a control. Export a scenario and reproduce the calculation in R.


Show the demo in the exercise rather than a separate application shell. Distinguish a simulated model truth from evidence available in an actual unknown. Ask whether recalibrating a straight line cures curvature; residuals reveal why it does not.

title: UV and visible absorption
section: Take the complete argument into the exercise
text:
Take the complete argument into the exercise

title: Quiz: electrodes and potentiometry
text:
Try each question before opening its hint. Then explain the answer in chemical and measurement terms. Lecture · Exercise.

Q1. A combined pH electrode contains one body. Does its potential no longer depend on a reference electrode or junction?






Hint





Packaging does not eliminate a cell function.









Answer





No. The indicator and reference functions are packaged together. The observed cell potential can still depend on reference/junction conditions. A high-input-impedance meter reads potential with negligible net measurement current.




Q2. An idealised calibration is \(E=200-60\log_{10}[c/(1\,\mathrm{mol/L})]\) mV. What concentration corresponds to 440 mV?






Hint





Solve for the log value, then undo the logarithm.









Answer





The log concentration is \((440-200)/(-60)=-4\). Thus \(c=10^{-4}\) mol/L. The value −4 itself is not a concentration.




Q3. pH rises by one unit. By what factor does hydrogen-ion activity change?






Hint





pH already contains the negative base-ten logarithm.









Answer





It decreases tenfold. pH is an activity quantity; interpreting it as ordinary mol/L concentration without an activity relation changes the claim.




Q4. An independent check error is +1.5 mV with acceptance ±2.0 mV. Is the calibration exact because the check passes?






Hint





A tolerance allows nonzero error.









Answer





No. It passes the stated exercise criterion, but the nonzero voltage error can still bias concentration. Its significance belongs in the performance/uncertainty evaluation; acceptance is not zero uncertainty.




Q5. A fluoride sample has half the calibration activity coefficient at the same concentration, with no drift. A check prepared under calibration conditions passes. What can happen to the sample inverse estimate?






Hint





The check does not share the sample-specific activity relation.









Answer





The sample has half the activity, so the old concentration calibration infers half its true free-ion concentration in this ideal model. A passing reference check does not establish sample-matrix transfer. A known mismatch needs investigation or appropriate matching/correction evidence.




Q6. Why do equal positive/negative voltage bounds generally become unequal concentration changes after inversion?






Hint





Invert each voltage limit separately.









Answer





Concentration depends exponentially on voltage. Equal voltage deviations give reciprocal multiplicative factors, not equal additive concentration differences. A voltage SD must not simply be relabelled as a concentration SD.

title: Exercise: electrodes and logarithmic calibration
text:
Background
A potentiometric cell measures an indicator/reference potential difference with negligible measurement current. Under a stated convention, \(E=K+(2.303RT/zF)\log_{10}a_i\), where \(a_i=\gamma_i c_i/c^\circ\) is dimensionless activity and \(z\) is signed charge. The ideal 25 °C monovalent magnitude is about 59.16 mV per decade; this fluoride convention has a negative slope.
A calibration using concentration assumes an appropriate activity relationship between samples and standards. Its model is \(E=a+b\log_{10}[c/(1\,\mathrm{mol/L})]\), hence \(c=10^{(E-a)/b}\) mol/L. Matched ionic strength can help but does not remove every interference. These data and all model truths are simulated.

  left_join(select(checks, block, check_pass), by = "block") |>

title: Exercise: electrodes and logarithmic calibration
text:
Hints






B1: undo the logarithm





At \(10^{-4}\) mol/L, the explanatory value is −4. After solving for the log concentration, raise 10 to that power.









B2: respect the negative slope





The ratio is \(10^{\Delta E/b}\), not \(\Delta E/b\) itself.









B3: activity ratio





The sample has half the activity at the same concentration. The check need not share the sample-specific activity coefficient.









B4: compare absolute errors





Subtract expected potential, then compare absolute errors with 2.00 mV. A nonzero error can lie inside the acceptance interval.









E1: the check has a different matrix





The reference is under calibration conditions. The sample-specific ratio does not change its response in this model.









E2: acceptance is not exactness





Both drifts change concentration. Only one exceeds the selected check tolerance.









E3: an ideal control is an assumption





The switch sets the ratio exactly to one. Real adjustment does not prove the absence of interfering ions, complexes or junction changes.









R1: finite explanatory values





log10 is undefined as a finite value at zero; changing the concentration unit changes the intercept convention.









R2: preserve evidence with IDs





Inspect both the check table and the joined unknown table. NA here is a withheld estimate, not zero fluoride.









R3: exponentiate both limits





The inverse is exponential. Equal positive/negative voltage deviations map to reciprocal concentration factors rather than equal additive concentration changes.

title: Exercise: electrodes and logarithmic calibration
text:
Solutions






Full worked solutions





B1. \(E=-97.42+(-59.16)(-4)=139.22\) mV. For 121.20 mV, \(\log_{10}[c/(1\,\mathrm{mol/L})]=(121.20+97.42)/(-59.16)\approx-3.6954\); \(c\approx2.016\times10^{-4}\) mol/L. The log value itself is not concentration. These hand coefficients are the ideal demo model, not the fitted dataset below.
B2. Factor \(10^{-17.8/(-59.16)}\approx1.999\). A lower fluoride potential means higher inferred concentration in this signed convention.
B3. The candidate is half the true free-ion concentration. A check under calibration matrix conditions still has ratio one and can pass. It therefore cannot establish this sample’s calibration transfer. The known mismatch should prevent a justified sample result until corrected or evaluated appropriately.
B4. Errors are +0.12 and +6.02 mV. The early check passes and later check fails. The early error is nevertheless nonzero: the rule permits a bounded error, not perfect accuracy.
E1. At ratio 0.50 and drift zero, candidate concentration is half the input, while the check passes. The true-input point lies on the shifted sample line; the inverse point lies on the old calibration at the same potential. Only the simulation exposes the true concentration.
E2. +1 mV passes but gives concentration factor \(10^{1/(-59.16)}\approx0.962\); +6 mV fails and gives factor about 0.792. Investigate the failure, establish satisfactory calibration/checks and remeasure affected samples. Do not assume the failed check identifies its cause or supplies a universal correction.
E3. Ideal matching sets the sample/standard activity-coefficient ratio to one. It does not model or eliminate interfering-ion effects, speciation, reference-junction changes, temperature effects or recovery. These remain chemical assumptions to evaluate rather than automatic consequences of a switch.
R1. Fitted intercept is −97.42 mV, slope −59.10 mV per decade for concentration in mol/L relative to 1 mol/L. Zero has no finite log value. Calibrating in another unit without altering the intercept gives the wrong inverse convention.
R2. The accepted early estimate is 1.99915 × 10⁻⁴ mol/L. The later +6.02 mV check error fails; its reported concentration is NA even though code can compute a candidate. The fixed matrix assumptions remain necessary for the early result; passing the check does not prove them for arbitrary samples.
R3. The fitted-data factor is \(10^{-17.8/(-59.10)}\approx2.001\):
factor_from_decrease <- 10^(-17.8 / b)
factor_from_decrease
For a voltage uncertainty bound \(\pm u_E\), multiplicative concentration factors are \(10^{\pm u_E/b}\). Their differences from one are unequal, producing asymmetric concentration limits. A voltage SD must not be relabelled as a concentration SD.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
About this lecture

Distinguish stoichiometric equivalence from an observed endpoint.
Calculate acid concentration and EDTA hardness on their stated bases.
Use pH curves and blank evidence to defend a result.


The exercise begins with pen-and-paper tasks, then embeds the exploratory model and finishes in R using the existing course datasets. Keep each numerical result connected to its chemical quantity. All data and profiles are simulated; the demonstrations do not validate actual instruments or preparation methods.

title: Equilibrium and titration
section: A known reagent counts an unknown amount
text:
A known reagent counts an unknown amount

What makes delivered volume chemically meaningful?

Known titrant concentration and reaction stoichiometry. The indicator or electrode estimates the endpoint; it does not replace the reaction.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Know the titrant concentration
A nominal concentration is not automatically a standardised concentration.

The example supplies standardised 0.1000 mol/L base. Real preparation and standardisation uncertainty belong in the result.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Read delivered volume

Delivered volume = final reading − initial reading.

An initial position need not be zero. Ask students what a burette reading records and why the final reading alone can be misleading.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Separate equivalence from endpoint

Equivalence is stoichiometric. The endpoint is observed or estimated.

An indicator, electrode or algorithm gives a procedure-defined estimate. Explain endpoint bias using a systematic overrun.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Write the reaction first
\mathrm{H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O}. One mole consumes one mole.

The concentration formula follows from the one-to-one stoichiometry. Other stoichiometries need their coefficients, not a memorised volume shortcut.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Calculate a worked acid concentration

c_a=c_b V_{eq}/V_a = 0.1000 × 25.00/25.00 = 0.1000 mol/L.

The acid aliquot is 25.00 mL. Supplied endpoint estimate is 25.00 mL. Explain when volumes may remain in matching millilitre units and when mole calculations require litres.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Explain the curve before equivalence

What species mainly determines pH here?

Excess strong acid. The ideal model also includes water equilibrium; it matters near equivalence.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Explain the curve after equivalence

What now controls pH?

Excess strong base. The total volume is changing, so excess amount is divided by the current solution volume.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Neutrality is conditional

This ideal strong-acid/strong-base equivalence has pH 7 at 25 °C.

It is not a universal endpoint rule. A weak acid will provide a counterexample.

title: Equilibrium and titration
section: Differentiate using the actual volume spacing
text:
Differentiate using the actual volume spacing

Finite difference: \Delta pH/\Delta V.

The supplied table has smaller additions near equivalence. Treating every step as one millilitre distorts the derivative.

title: Equilibrium and titration
section: A numerical maximum is not complete validation
text:
A numerical maximum is not complete validation

Noise and step spacing affect the slope peak.

Use the exploratory derivative to locate a region. A real endpoint method must be specified and evaluated against the chemical question.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Same amount, different equilibrium

Which acid requires more base at equivalence?

They have the same initial amount and one-to-one stoichiometry, so the equivalence volumes are equal. Acid strength changes the curve, not the supplied amount.

title: Equilibrium and titration
section: Choose an indicator for the actual curve
text:
Choose an indicator for the actual curve

A transition interval must lie in an appropriate steep region.

For the weak acid, conjugate base affects equivalence pH. Do not choose an indicator solely because its colour is easy to see.

title: Equilibrium and titration
section: The buffer region has a chemical cause
text:
The buffer region has a chemical cause

Weak acid and its conjugate base coexist before equivalence.

The comparison weak acid has supplied pKa 4.76. No exhaustive polyprotic derivation is needed for the core task.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
EDTA gives another stoichiometric count

One accessible metal ion consumes one EDTA ligand.

The simplified hardness case counts accessible calcium and magnesium. Other metals can interfere if they also consume EDTA.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
pH changes effective binding

Ligand protonation and metal side reactions affect the conditional equilibrium.

A large overall formation constant is not sufficient to establish performance under arbitrary acidity. Buffer and indicator belong to the procedure.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Name the reporting basis

Hardness as CaCO₃ uses an equivalent molar mass.

It does not establish that carbonate was present or separately identify calcium and magnesium. We supply molar mass 100.09 g/mol.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Correct the measured consumption

H1a: 6.30 − 0.10 − 0.05 = 6.15 mL.

The first two numbers are final and initial burette positions. The third is matched blank consumption, on the same delivered-volume basis.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Calculate the metal amount

0.01000 mol/L × 0.00615 L = 6.15 × 10⁻⁵ mol.

This amount refers to the 50.00 mL sample aliquot. Retain full precision and convert to the reporting equivalent only after establishing amount.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Convert to the sample basis

6.15 × 10⁻⁵ mol × 100.09 g/mol / 0.05000 L = 123.11 mg/L as CaCO₃.

Show the gram-to-milligram conversion explicitly in discussion.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Keep repeated preparations distinct

H1a and H1b are separate preparations of H1.

They probe preparation repeatability; they are not independent collected waters. H2a is another supplied sample.

title: Equilibrium and titration
section: What can bias a titration result?
text:
What can bias a titration result?

Endpoint overrun, wrong titrant concentration, blank consumption, interference.

Ask for the direction of error for one example. A forgotten positive blank consumption raises the result in this model.

title: Equilibrium and titration
text:
Transfer the reaction and basis

25.00 mL water; 4.10 mL delivered EDTA; 0.10 mL blank; 0.01000 mol/L.

Allow the calculation. Corrected four millilitres yields 160.14 mg/L as CaCO3. Require the reporting basis in the answer.

title: Quiz: calibration and quality control
text:
Try each question before opening its hint or answer. These practice questions check chemical reasoning and small calculations; they are not a graded question bank.

Q1. Standards set concentration and the instrument measures response. Which model direction matches this design: response ~ concentration or concentration ~ response?






Hint Q1





Place the observed error-bearing response on the left.









Answer Q1





Use response ~ concentration for the stated calibration model, then invert that fitted relation for an unknown. Reversing the least-squares regression is a different model, not an equivalent algebraic rearrangement.





Q2. For \(y=0.020+0.100c\) and unknown response 0.520, find c. Its preparation factor is four; what is the original concentration?






Hint Q2





Subtract intercept, divide by slope, then undo the preparation dilution.









Answer Q2





\(c_f=(0.520-0.020)/0.100=5.00\) mg/L final; original is 20.0 mg/L if factor four and the chemical preparation model are valid.





Q3. At a known standard, observed response is 0.310 and fitted response 0.330. What is its residual? Does that sign identify the cause?






Hint Q3





Residual is observed minus fitted.









Answer Q3





Residual is −0.020 response units: the observation lies below the fitted line. The sign alone does not distinguish preparation error, noise, instrument behaviour or another cause.





Q4. R² is 0.999 but residuals show a clear curved pattern. Does the high R² justify the straight line over that range?






Hint Q4





A summary of association is not a check of every model assumption.









Answer Q4





No. Systematic residual structure is evidence that the line misses part of the response relation. Investigate a justified range or alternative validated model rather than deleting inconvenient observations to improve appearance.





Q5. An independently sourced 5.00 mg/L check is estimated as 4.00 mg/L. The supplied acceptance window is 95–105%. What should happen?






Hint Q5





Calculate recovery, then apply the preselected rule.









Answer Q5





Recovery is 80%, so the affected measurement block fails this exercise rule. Withhold affected sample results, investigate, restore satisfactory calibration/checks and remeasure. Do not automatically divide all samples by 0.80 without establishing the cause.





Q6. An unknown signal is above the largest calibrated response. Can changing its recorded dilution factor without a new measurement establish its concentration?






Hint Q6





What new evidence has been acquired?









Answer Q6





No. A justified new dilution must actually be prepared and measured within the supported range. Editing metadata on an old reading does not supply a new response and cannot validate extrapolation.





Q7. A blank SD is 0.002 response units and sensitivity 0.250 response units per mg/L. What is the indicative 3-SD concentration increment?






Hint Q7





Use \(3s/b\), and keep the heuristic’s scope explicit.









Answer Q7





\(3(0.002)/0.250=0.024\) mg/L. It is an illustrative blank-relative increment, not universal detection-method validation. Procedure, matrix, decision probabilities and noise assumptions still matter; below limit is not exactly zero analyte.





Q8. Why does uncertainty in an inferred concentration include more than the SD of its repeated responses?






Hint Q8





The inverse uses fitted slope and intercept as well as the new mean response.









Answer Q8





Slope and intercept are estimated and correlated. Their covariance propagates through the inverse relation, along with new response variability. Preparation volumes, stock concentrations, recovery and sampling may add further contributions. A forward-response interval alone is not a concentration interval.

Background
