title: Exercise: calibration and quality control
text:
Hints






Hint B1





Subtract the fitted intercept before dividing by slope. Then reverse the preparation dilution to return to the original basis.









Hint B2





Compare \(0.510/0.200\) with \((0.510-0.010)/0.200\). A response can have a background offset even at nominal concentration zero.









Hint B3





Residual is observed minus fitted. The sign locates a point relative to a line; it does not identify a chemical or instrumental mechanism by itself.









Hint B4





Recovery is \(100\times c_{estimated}/c_{reference}\). Apply the preselected rule before deciding on a reportable result.









Hint B5





Use \(3s/b\). A complete detection procedure also needs its noise, blank, matrix and decision-probability conditions.









Hints E1–E4





Range, independent QC and residual review are separate requirements. A simulator can expose the generating truth, but a real unknown cannot be validated merely by looking at a hidden correct answer.









Hint R1





lm() fits absorbance as response. Prepared concentration is the explanatory variable. Volume/preparation records connect final solution to original sample.









Hint R2





The helper propagates reading noise and the fitted intercept/slope covariance through an inverse relation. It excludes preparation and recovery effects.









Hint R3





residuals() can show curvature despite a high overall association. A justified range needs adequate standards and checks for the intended sample responses.









Hint R4





Including the check in calibration sacrifices its independent role. Filter by role, not by row position or whichever rows make the result look best.

title: Exercise: calibration and quality control
text:
Solutions






Solutions B1–B5





B1. \((0.510-0.010)/0.200=2.50\) mg/L final; original concentration is \(2.50\times5=12.5\) mg/L. Both units and material stage belong in the report.
B2. A forced-zero calculation gives 2.55 mg/L final, 2% above 2.50 mg/L. A nominal zero concentration does not guarantee a precisely zero response. The intercept must follow the justified model and evidence, not convenience.
B3. \(0.440-0.410=+0.030\) signal units. The point lies above the fitted line. One residual alone does not establish its cause; a pattern across concentration may support investigation of model failure.
B4. Recovery is \(100(1.70/2.00)=85.0\%\), failing the supplied 95–105% rule. Withhold affected unknowns, investigate, restore satisfactory calibration/checks and remeasure as appropriate. Dividing all results by 0.85 would assume a cause not established by the failed check.
B5. \(3(0.004)/0.500=0.024\) mg/L is a rough blank-relative concentration increment. It is not universal validation, and a below-limit response is not proof of exactly zero analyte.









Solutions E1–E4





E1. A model review has not yet been made, so a numerical candidate is not automatically reportable. With q=0, noise=0, accepted review and satisfactory range/QC, a=0.010 and b=0.200 give 2.50 mg/L final and 5.00 mg/L original.
E2. Positive q gives diminishing sensitivity and systematic residual structure despite high \(R^2\). Rejecting the line withholds the simple estimate. A narrower range may reduce nonlinearity, but needs adequate standards, diagnostics, independent checks and suitable intended sample responses; it is not validated by removing inconvenient points.
E3. At factor 1 the final concentration is 20 mg/L, beyond the four mg/L calibration. A new factor-10 measurement gives 2 mg/L final and returns to 20 mg/L original. It supplies a new observed response; changing a number beside the old out-of-range response supplies no new measurement.
E4. Under the linear zero-noise model a −20% sensitivity change gives an independent-check recovery of 80%, so affected samples are withheld. The old calibration residuals still look perfect because they predate the change.









Solutions R1–R4





R1. a≈0.003873883 absorbance units; b≈0.198799368 L/mg Fe. Final estimate is 2.3981269 mg Fe/L. The residuals lack obvious curvature in this selected range, though that does not prove sample recovery or selectivity. Original-water concentration also needs the actual aliquot and final-volume factor.
R2. The supplied helper gives standard uncertainty about 0.0045090 mg Fe/L and approximate 95% interval 2.388568–2.407686 mg Fe/L final. It assumes a correct linear model, independent normal equal-variance response errors, negligible calibration-concentration uncertainty and a well-determined positive slope. Sampling, volume uncertainty, matrix bias and recovery are omitted. A forward interval has response units; inverse concentration limits require the uncertain inverse relation, including intercept/slope covariance. The helper uses a first-order approximation, not a general nonlinear inverse algorithm.
R3. Curved-response residuals show a systematic concentration pattern. This is evidence against the single straight-line model over that full range, not permission to erase standards until \(R^2\) looks satisfactory. A proposed range or model needs independent evidence and fit to the analytical purpose.
R4. filter(role == "standard") reproduces the fitted coefficients within numerical rounding. The check material tests whether the selected calibration predicts an independently known quantity; fitting it into the same line would reduce its ability to reveal failure. Unknown rows do not supply known calibration concentrations in an actual analysis.

title: Error and uncertainty
text:
Which method would you trust?

The reference is 10.00 mg/L. Compare both location and spread.

Ask for a justification before naming precision or bias. The series are repeat measurements of the same reference material.

title: Error and uncertainty
text:
Precision concerns repeated results

A and B both have SD ≈ 0.0158 mg/L.

Their repeatability is similar. Precision requires stated conditions; repeatability is not the same as all possible between-day or between-laboratory variation.

title: Error and uncertainty
text:
Bias concerns a suitable reference

B mean = 10.50 mg/L: estimated bias +0.50 mg/L.

Reference uncertainty is neglected only in this teaching comparison. A precise series can be displaced.

title: Error and uncertainty
section: A mean close to the reference is not a guarantee
text:
A mean close to the reference is not a guarantee

C mean = 10.00 mg/L, but its SD ≈ 0.316 mg/L.

An accidentally close mean in five readings does not validate a method across samples and matrices.

title: Error and uncertainty
section: Uncertainty describes doubt under a model
text:
Uncertainty describes doubt under a model
It is not the observed difference from a secretly known true value.

A measurement model relates inputs to the reported quantity. Uncertainty requires relevant input uncertainties and their dependencies.

title: Error and uncertainty
text:
Retrieve grouped summaries
summarise(n = n(), mean_mg_l = mean(measured_mg_l),
          sd_mg_l = sd(measured_mg_l))

Ask students to interpret the units of SD and variance. SD has the concentration unit; variance has its square.

title: Error and uncertainty
section: Spread of readings and uncertainty in a mean differ
text:
Spread of readings and uncertainty in a mean differ
For independent stable readings: u_{reading}(\bar x)=s/\sqrt n.

Name the quantity carefully. This is the reading contribution to the mean, not the SD of future individual readings.

title: Error and uncertainty
section: Do not divide shared effects by square root of n
text:
Do not divide shared effects by square root of n

A stock error is shared by every reading made from that stock.

Trace the graph from stock through prepared aliquot to repeated readings. Identify which information new readings do and do not add.

title: Error and uncertainty
text:
More readings approach a floor

Which curve keeps decreasing? Which levels off?

Solid combines reading uncertainty with a shared 0.10 mg/L component; dashed shows reading alone. These numbers are an independent illustration.

title: Error and uncertainty
section: Choose the quantity before choosing the formula
text:
Choose the quantity before choosing the formula

One collected sample, several preparations and several readings need different treatment.

The experimental unit comes first. Do not turn dependent data into independent evidence by running a familiar formula.

title: Error and uncertainty
text:
Write the dilution model

c=c_sV_a/V_f.

Inputs: stock one hundred mg/L, aliquot five millilitres, final fifty millilitres. The result is ten mg/L.

title: Error and uncertainty
section: Use standard uncertainties of the inputs
text:
Use standard uncertainties of the inputs
Stock: 0.4 mg/L; aliquot: 0.006 mL; final volume: 0.03 mL.

They are supplied standard uncertainties, not tolerance bounds. If only a tolerance is available, a justified distribution model is needed before treating it as standard uncertainty.

title: Error and uncertainty
section: Propagate each contribution onto the output scale
text:
Propagate each contribution onto the output scale

Stock contributes 0.040 mg/L.

Use concentration times relative stock uncertainty. All contributions must refer to the reported concentration before combining.

title: Error and uncertainty
text:
Volume contributions also survive averaging

Aliquot: 0.012 mg/L; final volume: 0.006 mg/L.

Taking additional readings of the prepared flask does not remeasure its actual volume.

title: Error and uncertainty
text:
Combine independent contributions in quadrature

u(c)=\sqrt{0.040^2+0.012^2+0.006^2} = 0.04219 mg/L.

The square-root-of-squares rule here assumes independent inputs and a valid first-order approximation. Correlated volumes require covariance terms.

title: Error and uncertainty
text:
Improve the dominant source first

Would a more precise final flask solve most of this budget?

No: the stock is dominant in this particular example. Do not treat this ranking as universal.

title: Error and uncertainty
section: Averaging is useful within its scope
text:
Averaging is useful within its scope

More independent readings reduce the reading component.

Show both curves again and ask where new preparation information would enter. This is not an argument against replication, but for appropriate replication.

title: Error and uncertainty
text:
An interval needs a meaning
Standard uncertainty u; expanded uncertainty U=ku; confidence interval for a mean.

Ask which one the previous number represents. It is a standard uncertainty. Do not label every plus/minus quantity as ninety-five percent.

title: Error and uncertainty
section: A small-sample mean uses its sampling model
text:
A small-sample mean uses its sampling model
\bar x\pm t_{0.975,n-1}s/\sqrt n.

This interval assumes independent readings under an appropriate normal model. It does not supply sampling or recovery uncertainty missing from the measurement design.

title: Error and uncertainty
section: Treat a known bias as a problem to investigate
text:
Treat a known bias as a problem to investigate

An arbitrary error bar does not correct a systematically displaced method.

A justified bias correction has its own uncertainty. Ask which evidence would support correction rather than automatically recentering every dataset.

title: Error and uncertainty
section: Report precision that the uncertainty supports
text:
Report precision that the uncertainty supports
10.000 mg/L; standard uncertainty 0.042 mg/L under the stated model.

Retain full numerical precision in code. Round in the report consistently with uncertainty and purpose. State omitted sources.

title: Error and uncertainty
text:
Transfer: halve the stock uncertainty

Replace 0.4 by 0.2 mg/L. What happens to combined uncertainty?

New standard uncertainty is 0.02408 mg/L, not exactly half of 0.04219 because other components remain.

title: Error and uncertainty
section: What still lies outside the budget?
text:
What still lies outside the budget?

Sampling, recovery, matrix effects and unmodelled preparation variation.

Connect this list to the measurand. An uncertainty estimate can be arithmetically correct but incomplete for the decision.

title: Quiz: sampling and preparation
text:
Try each question before opening its hint or answer. These practice questions check chemical reasoning and small calculations; they are not a graded question bank.

Q1. A solid has equal-mass strata with means 5, 10 and 30 mg/kg. What is its bulk mean? What target does top-only sampling approach?






Hint Q1





Use the material mass weights, then consider which stratum was actually collected.









Answer Q1





The bulk mean is \((5+10+30)/3=15\) mg/kg. Top-only grabs approach the top mean of 5 mg/kg under this model. Smaller top-only scatter does not supply information about the rest of the solid.





Q2. The same strata instead have mass fractions 0.20, 0.30 and 0.50. What is the bulk mean?






Hint Q2





Multiply each concentration by its corresponding mass fraction.









Answer Q2





\(0.20(5)+0.30(10)+0.50(30)=19\) mg/kg. An equal-stratum average would target three equal masses and is no longer appropriate. The weights must refer to the defined material, not convenience.





Q3. A 1.000 g material gives 50.00 mL extract. A 5.00 mL aliquot made to 25.00 mL reads 2.00 mg/L. Find extracted analyte in mg/g.






Hint Q3





Undo the aliquot dilution, find total extracted mass, then divide by original mass.









Answer Q3





The extract is \(2.00(25/5)=10.0\) mg/L. It contains \(10.0(0.05000)=0.500\) mg; divided by 1.000 g gives 0.500 mg/g extracted. Complete native recovery still needs evidence.





Q4. With D=4, 20 mL aqueous and 5 mL extracting phase, what is the ideal recovered fraction?






Hint Q4





Use \(DV_o/(V_a+DV_o)\).









Answer Q4





\(4(5)/(20+4(5))=0.50\), or 50%. D is a concentration ratio; recovery also depends on phase volumes. This assumes equilibrium, immiscibility, unchanged volumes and no other loss.





Q5. Why can two fresh solvent extractions recover more than one extraction using the same total solvent?






Hint Q5





After removing each extracting phase, the next fresh portion repartitions the analyte left behind.









Answer Q5





Each fresh portion establishes a new equilibrium with the remaining analyte. The fractions left after each step multiply. This can improve ideal recovery without adding more total solvent, but does not prove real recovery if equilibration or separation fails.





Q6. A post-extraction spike recovers 100%. What claim about native extraction remains unsupported?






Hint Q6





Identify the steps the added analyte skipped.









Answer Q6





Complete recovery of native analyte before spike addition remains unsupported. The spike did not undergo that extraction, and even a pre-extraction freely dissolved spike may not represent native bound material.





Q7. Does one composite made from ten increments count as ten independent samples for estimating spatial variation?






Hint Q7





What happened to the original increment identities and separate measurements?









Answer Q7





No. The composite is one combined material under its specified weighting design. It can support a bulk quantity, but it does not preserve ten independent measured spatial results or their original variation.





Q8. Why might a treatment useful for retaining an element in solution be unsuitable for preserving its original oxidation states?






Hint Q8





Different measurands require different chemical information to survive.









Answer Q8





A preservation treatment can prevent precipitation or surface loss while changing speciation. The result must match the intended elemental amount or species quantity and the specified preparation. There is no universally suitable preservation treatment for every measurand.

title: Exercise: sampling and preparation
text:
Background
A heterogeneous solid has three equal-mass strata with mean iron concentrations 8, 14 and 25 mg/kg. Its bulk mass mean weights the strata by mass, not by the number of convenient grabs. A composite can estimate a bulk quantity but no longer preserves every original spatial difference.
For a caffeine extraction, the concentration in the measured flask must be returned through aliquot and extract volumes to the original mass:
\[w_{extracted}=c_{final}\frac{V_{final}}{V_{aliquot}}
\frac{V_{extract}}{m_{sample}}.\]
Use litres for \(V_{extract}\) when \(c\) is mg/L. The result is extracted caffeine; complete native-analyte recovery is not established. For ideal immiscible phases, \(D=c_o/c_a\) and the fraction remaining after n equal fresh extractions using total solvent \(V_o\) is \([V_a/(V_a+D V_o/n)]^n\).

title: Exercise: sampling and preparation
text:
Hints






Hint B1





For equal masses, average stratum means. Repeating a biased selection changes random scatter but not the material left unsampled.









Hint B2





Multiply each concentration by its material mass fraction, then sum. Fractions must refer to the intended target and add to one.









Hint B3





Undo the final dilution first, multiply by the total extract in litres, then divide the extracted mg by original grams.









Hint B4





For one extraction, the fraction left is \(20/(20+9\times10)\). For two, multiply the fraction left after each fresh 5 mL extraction.









Hint B5





A late spike does not pass through earlier losses. Even an early freely dissolved spike may not behave like native bound material.









Hints E1–E4





Changing sample allocation changes the weighting of a pooled average. In the extraction experiment, keep total solvent fixed; every portion is fresh, phases equilibrate and are separated completely in this ideal model.









Hint R1





The raw table contains four grabs from each equal-mass stratum. Balanced counts make the arithmetic coincide. Unequal counts generally break that coincidence.









Hint R2





mg/L × L gives mg, then mg/g uses original sample grams. The final flask and original solid do not have interchangeable concentration units.









Hint R3





Use \((1.50\times10/1)\times0.04000/0.4000\) and identify which losses are assumed absent. The formula alone does not demonstrate them absent.









Hint R4





group_by() separates stratum summaries. An unsampled stratum has unknown concentration, not a measured zero. A bulk estimate needs its evidence or a justified model.

title: Exercise: sampling and preparation
text:
Solutions






Solutions B1–B5





B1. \((8+14+25)/3=15.667\) mg/kg. Top-only sampling approaches 8 mg/kg. A small repeat SD describes the top measurements, not the bias from excluding other material.
B2. \(0.50(8)+0.30(14)+0.20(25)=13.2\) mg/kg. Equal weights would represent three equal masses that no longer exist in this new target.
B3. Final-to-extract factor \(10/2=5\) gives 9.60 mg/L extract. Amount is \(9.60\times0.02500=0.240\) mg; divided by 0.5000 g it gives 0.480 mg/g extracted.
B4. One recovery \(1-20/110=0.81818\); two recoveries together give \(1-(20/65)^2=0.90533\). This assumes constant distribution ratio and phase volumes, equilibrium, complete separation and fresh solvent for each extraction, with no reaction or handling loss. It is not validation of real native extraction.
B5. No. The late spike tests incremental behaviour after it was added, not native analyte lost before addition. A native bound analyte can differ from a freely dissolved spike, so equivalence also needs evidence.









Solutions E1–E4





E1. With equal grab counts, the two averages agree. Twenty top plus three middle and three bottom grabs make the naive average target \((20\times8+3\times14+3\times25)/26=10.654\) mg/kg in expectation. The average of the three stratum means remains near 15.667 mg/kg and uses the supplied mass weights. Exact simulated results vary with run.
E2. The full bulk quantity cannot be estimated from all strata by this procedure because middle and bottom are absent. Top-only precision cannot supply their concentrations. The demo withholds the stratified estimate rather than inventing zeros.
E3. The realised grabs and estimated means vary. The defined equal-mass target and the rule for weighting strata remain fixed. More independent grabs reduce random variation under this model but do not justify a different sampling target.
E4. Recoveries are 81.8% and 90.5%. Lower D leaves more analyte in the aqueous phase. Several fresh extractions improve this ideal equilibrium recovery, but bound analyte, reaction, emulsion, incomplete equilibration or handling loss can invalidate the ideal assumptions.









Solutions R1–R4





R1. Supplied stratum means are 8, 14 and 25 mg/kg. Equal counts and equal stratum masses make the pooled mean equal the equal-stratum mean. The three caffeine results are 0.480, 0.490 and 0.750 mg/g. Recovery calculations match B4.
R2. /1000 converts extract mL into L. extract_mg_l refers to the extract; extracted_mg is amount in its total volume; caffeine_mg_g refers to original solid mass. Reporting 1.92 mg/L final as 1.92 mg/g confuses quantities and ignores the preparation chain.
R3. \(1.50\times10=15.0\) mg/L extract; \(15.0\times0.04000=0.600\) mg; \(0.600/0.4000=1.50\) mg/g extracted. This still assumes valid measured concentration and no transfer loss, and does not establish complete native recovery.
R4. R reproduces the demo’s all-grab mean and equal mean of stratum means when all three strata appear. Missing rows for a stratum mean it was not sampled. Replacing that missing evidence with zero would create a false bulk estimate.

title: From sample to answer
section: A number needs a chemical question
text:
A number needs a chemical question

What quantity will our result describe?

Ask for quantity, material scope and unit before naming an instrument. Use a bottle of water as the concrete example.

title: From sample to answer
text:
Separate analyte from matrix

Chloride is the analyte. Water and other dissolved components form the matrix.

The matrix is not necessarily inert. It can change selectivity, recovery or response.

title: From sample to answer
section: The same sample can answer different questions
text:
The same sample can answer different questions

Conductivity and chloride concentration are different measurands.

Ask whether higher conductivity proves more chloride. Several mobile ionic species contribute. A calibration for one property cannot be transferred without a chemical relation.

title: From sample to answer
text:
Include place and time

A result from the supplied bottle is not automatically a river-wide mean.

Ask students what claim is justified if all material came from a single location at one time. This introduces sampling without inventing a representative design.

title: From sample to answer
text:
Preparation belongs in the definition

Filtered iron, unfiltered iron and original Fe(II) need different evidence.

Filtration changes material entering the procedure; reduction changes species. Later lessons will make the assumptions explicit.

title: From sample to answer
text:
Qualitative and quantitative claims
Identity: what evidence supports the substance?
Amount: what relates the selective response to a quantity?

A peak at an expected retention time is evidence, but coelution is possible. Amount needs both identification/selectivity and a suitable response calibration.

title: From sample to answer
text:
Follow the result backwards

Which record connects this reported concentration to the collected material?

Trace question, collected sample, preparation, signal, calibration and back-calculation. R cannot repair a missing preparation record.

title: From sample to answer
section: One row means one collected sample
text:
One row means one collected sample

Eight rows: four inlet samples and four outlet samples.

These are simulated independent collected samples in the teaching design. They are not before/after pairs merely because row positions can be matched.

title: From sample to answer
text:
Retrieve the familiar import
water <- read_csv("data/course/water.csv")
glimpse(water)

Check types, IDs, units, missing values and the experimental unit. Keep raw data unchanged. Use the R project to establish relative paths.

title: From sample to answer
text:
Show the observations first

What is the difference between the locations? What variation remains?

Means are 19.5 and 12.5 mg/L. Individual observations make sample size and spread visible. Do not jump to a p-value.

title: From sample to answer
text:
Summarise with a count
water |> group_by(location) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_mg_l = mean(chloride_mg_l))

Read the numerical means as summaries of four collected samples each. A count of missing results would also be necessary in incomplete data.

title: From sample to answer
text:
Make a restrained claim

The descriptive difference is 7.0 mg/L for these samples.

Ask what additional sampling would support a broader temporal or spatial claim. The available design does not establish a treatment effect.

title: From sample to answer
text:
Concentration is amount per volume

c=m/V; therefore m=cV.

Before revealing the example, ask whether taking a larger volume changes concentration or collected amount. Assume a homogeneous solution.

title: From sample to answer
text:
Calculate the collected amount

20.0 mg/L × 0.250 L = 5.00 mg.

Cancel litres explicitly. At unchanged concentration, a half-litre portion would contain ten milligrams.

title: From sample to answer
section: Convert the unit and the number together

Convert the unit and the number together
20 mg/L = 0.020 g/L.

A thousand-fold conversion error is not fixed by additional decimal places. Keep units in labels and the dictionary.

title: From sample to answer
section: A different graph answers a different question
text:
A different graph answers a different question

This axis is amount in a collected portion, not concentration.

All portions are 0.250 L here. If volumes varied, amount comparisons could differ from concentration comparisons.

Keep evidence portable

Raw data → saved code → derived table → rendered report.

Restart R and render. A console-only object makes a report dependent on session history. Reproducibility preserves reasoning; it does not guarantee the reasoning is correct.

0.0750 mg in 25.00 mL. What is the concentration?

Allow a calculation before answering: 3.00 mg/L. Then ask what is missing for a location-wide mean and an uncertainty statement.

text:
What would make this conclusion wrong?
Name one sampling, chemical and computing failure.

Possible answers: top-only sampling; nonspecific response; wrong volume unit or unmatched preparation record. Recover the whole argument, not a list of commands.

install.packages(c("readr", "dplyr", "ggplot2", "knitr", "rmarkdown"))

Read a lesson’s code from top to bottom in a fresh session. Run R in the R console, not a shell terminal. Keep raw CSV files unchanged. Units and row meanings are specified in the course data dictionary.

title: R reference for analytical measurements
text:
Inspect before calculating

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
x <- read_csv("data/course/water.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
glimpse(x)
names(x)
head(x)
sum(is.na(x$chloride_mg_l))
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(x$sample_id))

stopifnot() stops the script if its condition is false. Here it prevents mistaking duplicate IDs for independent collected samples. A failed check calls for inspection; it is not a command to delete rows automatically.

title: R reference for analytical measurements
text:
Calculate and summarise

x <- x |> mutate(chloride_mg = chloride_mg_l * collected_l)
x |> group_by(location) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_mg_l = mean(chloride_mg_l),
            sd_mg_l = sd(chloride_mg_l), .groups = "drop")

|> passes a result to the next function. mutate() adds derived columns. group_by() identifies groups for summarise(). Describe how missing values are handled and count them; na.rm = TRUE does not justify ignoring missingness.

title: R reference for analytical measurements
text:
Attach a preparation by ID
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(preparations$preparation_id),
          all(readings$preparation_id %in% preparations$preparation_id))
joined <- readings |>
  left_join(preparations, by = "preparation_id")
This example assumes the two tables have been imported in the relevant lesson. left_join() uses matching IDs, not row position. Unique preparation keys avoid multiplying rows; checking matches avoids losing the volume or mass needed for a calculation. Inspect row count and missing values afterwards.

title: R reference for analytical measurements
section: Fit a line and respect its direction
text:
Fit a line and respect its direction
fit <- lm(response ~ known_concentration, data = standards)
coef(fit)
residuals(fit)
The response is on the left. An inverse concentration estimate uses the fitted response relationship; fitting the variables in the opposite direction is a different regression. Inspect residuals, range and QC before exporting results.

title: R reference for analytical measurements
text:
Logarithms and differences

log10(0.0001)
10^(-4)
diff(c(0, 1, 1.5, 2))

log10() gives a base-ten logarithm; 10^x reverses it. The logarithm of a physical quantity is taken relative to a stated reference/unit convention. diff() gives consecutive differences. A titration derivative divides the pH differences by the corresponding volume differences, not by the number of rows.

title: R reference for analytical measurements
text:
Save the evidence

fig <- ggplot(x, aes(location, chloride_mg_l)) + geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Sampling location", y = "Chloride (mg/L)") + theme_minimal()
ggsave("output/water-plot.png", plot = fig, width = 7, height = 4)
write_csv(x, "output/water-results.csv")

Keep the source report at the root. Render from the console, outside the report:
rmarkdown::render("course-report.Rmd", output_dir = "reports")
An object-not-found error can mean a misspelling or a missing earlier step. A file-not-found error usually calls for checking project, relative path and filename. If Knit fails while Console succeeds, check for hidden session state. Restart R and rebuild from saved inputs rather than manually repairing the HTML.

title: Analytical chemistry glossary
text: The quantity intended to be measured, including the analyte, material and concentration or amount basis.

title: Analytical chemistry glossary
text: The quantity intended to be measured, including the analyte, material and concentration or amount basis.

title: Analytical chemistry glossary
text:
Sample
Material selected from a defined population or lot. Repeated readings of one preparation are not additional collected samples.

title: Analytical chemistry glossary
text:
Aliquot
A measured portion taken from a sample or solution.

title: Analytical chemistry glossary
text:
Dilution factor
Final total volume divided by aliquot volume, when dilution conserves analyte and volumes share units.

title: Analytical chemistry glossary
text:
Calibration
An established relationship between a measured response and known input quantities under specified conditions.

title: Analytical chemistry glossary
text:
Residual
Observed response minus the response predicted by the fitted model.

title: Analytical chemistry glossary
text:
Precision
Agreement among repeated measurements under specified conditions; it does not establish freedom from bias.

title: Analytical chemistry glossary
text:
Bias
An estimate of systematic departure from a reference quantity.

title: Analytical chemistry glossary
text:
Standard uncertainty
An uncertainty expressed as a standard deviation within a stated measurement model.

title: Analytical chemistry glossary
text:
Recovery
A measured quantity relative to a known added or reference quantity, with the preparation and concentration basis stated.

title: Analytical chemistry glossary
text:
Matrix effect
A change in analyte response caused by other sample components.

title: Analytical chemistry glossary
text:
Quality control
Checks, including method blanks and independent reference materials, used to assess whether the measurement process meets stated criteria. A passing check does not establish every aspect of method validity.

title: Analytical chemistry glossary
text:
Activity
A dimensionless effective concentration, for example \(a=\gamma c/c^\circ\) in a specified concentration convention. An electrode responds to activity under the stated model; matching conditions may permit calibration in concentration.

title: Analytical chemistry glossary
text:
Equivalence point
The titrant amount satisfying the chosen reaction stoichiometry.

title: Analytical chemistry glossary
text:
Endpoint
The observed experimental criterion used to locate completion; it can differ from equivalence.

title: Analytical chemistry glossary
text:
Absorbance
The negative base-ten logarithm of transmittance, A = −log₁₀(I/I₀).

title: Analytical chemistry glossary
text:
Retention time
Elapsed time between injection and the defined peak location in a chromatogram.

title: Analytical chemistry glossary
text:
Resolution
A measure of separation relative to peak widths; state the width convention when calculating it.

title: Analytical chemistry glossary
text:
Internal standard
A deliberately added reference compound used to normalize response. It corrects only effects that it shares appropriately with the analyte.

title: Analytical chemistry glossary
text:
Selectivity
The extent to which the procedure measures the intended analyte in the presence of other components.

title: Exercise: the analytical question
text:
Background
A measurand names the intended quantity, material and conditions. Here it is chloride mass concentration in supplied collected water, in mg chloride/L. The analyte is chloride; the matrix contains water and other species. A measured signal becomes this quantity only through a suitable chemical measurement model.
For a homogeneous solution, \(c=m/V\) and \(m=cV\). If no analyte is lost or added, dilution gives \(c_f=c_oV_a/V_f\). Final volume means the total after preparation, including solvent and reagents. The collected material, aliquot and final flask are different stages; name the stage in a reported concentration.

title: Exercise: the analytical question
text:
By hand
B1. The analysis establishes 0.0750 mg chloride in a 25.00 mL portion. Calculate concentration in mg/L. What information would still be needed to claim a location-wide mean? Hint
B2. A homogeneous solution is 20.0 mg/L. Calculate the analyte amount in (a) 0.250 L and (b) 0.500 L. Does its concentration change when a larger portion is taken? Hint
B3. A 10.00 mL aliquot is made to 50.00 mL total. The final concentration is 0.800 mg/L. Find the original concentration and analyte amount in the aliquot. Hint
B4. Four inlet samples give 18, 20, 19 and 21 mg/L; four outlet samples give 12, 13, 11 and 14 mg/L. Calculate both means and their difference. State one supported descriptive claim and one unsupported causal claim. Hint

title: Exercise: the analytical question
text:
Hints






Hint B1





Convert millilitres to litres before dividing. One portion supplies no sampling design for an entire location or time period.









Hint B2





Use \(m=cV\) with litres. The intensive concentration remains fixed when a larger portion of a homogeneous solution is taken.









Hint B3





The preparation factor is final total volume divided by aliquot volume. Calculate amount either before or after dilution; it should agree.









Hint B4





Average each set separately. The observations are from collected waters; they do not establish a treatment assignment, matching or representative temporal design.









Hint B5





Conductivity responds to several mobile ionic species. Reproducing a calculation does not establish that its chemical model is selective enough.









Hints E1–E4





Track \(c\), \(V\) and \(m\) separately. Changing aliquot volume at fixed dilution factor changes both original and final volumes proportionally. Adding solvent at fixed aliquot does not add analyte.









Hint R1





summarise() returns one summary per location after group_by(). Matching is a design property, not a coincidence of table positions.









Hint R2





Dividing mg/L by 1000 changes to g/L; multiplying mg/L by collected L gives mg.









Hint R3





Say what was observed, how many collected samples support it, and which place and time scope is actually given. Do not invent representativeness.









Hint R4





The /1000 converts mL to L. Consider transfer loss, adsorption, reaction or analyte in the added solvent.

title: Exercise: the analytical question
text:
Solutions






Solutions B1–B5





B1. \(0.0750/0.02500=3.00\) mg/L. A location-wide mean also needs a sampling design defining the location/time population and how portions represent it; the amount calculation supplies neither that design nor measurement uncertainty.
B2. \(20.0\times0.250=5.00\) mg and \(20.0\times0.500=10.0\) mg. Concentration is still 20.0 mg/L. Taking more solution changes collected amount, not the composition of a homogeneous solution.
B3. Factor \(50.00/10.00=5\); original \(0.800\times5=4.00\) mg/L. The aliquot contains \(4.00\times0.01000=0.0400\) mg, equal to \(0.800\times0.05000\) mg in the final flask. “Add 50 mL solvent” would describe a different volume.
B4. Inlet mean \((18+20+19+21)/4=19.5\) mg/L; outlet mean \((12+13+11+14)/4=12.5\) mg/L. Difference 7.0 mg/L. The sampled outlet waters have a lower observed mean. The data do not establish that a treatment caused this change, or that every outlet sample at another time would be lower.
B5. A justified relation between conductivity and chloride in the proposed matrix is missing. Other ions can alter conductivity without the same chloride change. A reproducible wrong model remains wrong; R does not establish selectivity.









Solutions E1–E4





E1. Original 20 mg/L; original aliquot amount 5 mg; final concentration 10 mg/L in 500 mL. Each statement names a different quantity or stage.
E2. A 500 mL aliquot contains 10 mg and becomes 1000 mL at factor 2. Final concentration remains 10 mg/L because amount and final volume doubled together.
E3. At 250 mL and factor 5 the final volume is 1250 mL, final concentration 4 mg/L and amount still 5 mg. \(4\times5=20\) mg/L returns to the original basis. At zero original chloride, amount and final concentration remain zero for every volume; missing evidence in a real sample would not justify entering zero.
E4. concentration_mg_l and volume_ml change; analyte_mg is conserved. Each row satisfies \(m=cV/1000\) when V is in mL. The ideal equality assumes no chemical or transfer change.









Solutions R1–R4





R1. Both locations have four collected samples; means match B4. Their sample SDs are about 1.291 mg/L. No matching variable or paired design is supplied; row order cannot create pairs.
R2. W2 is 20 mg/L, equivalent to 0.020 g/L. Its 0.250 L portion contains 5.00 mg. The first is concentration with a changed mass unit; the second is amount in a specified portion.
R3. One suitable paragraph is: “The four sampled inlet waters averaged 19.5 mg chloride/L and the four outlet waters 12.5 mg/L, an observed difference of 7.0 mg/L. Individual observations retain within-location spread. The supplied design does not establish causation or a broader time/location population mean.”
R4. The exported values reproduce the conservation equation up to floating- point rounding. Adsorption to a vessel, incomplete transfer or chemical loss could break it; contaminated solvent could add analyte. A small computational rounding tolerance is not an analytical acceptance criterion.

Where this leads
Sampling and preparation asks whether the aliquot represents the intended material and whether analyte recovery is complete. Keep sample identity, material scope and units through every later calibration and instrument result.

title: Quiz: the analytical question
text:
Try each question before opening its hint or answer. These practice questions check chemical reasoning and small calculations; they are not a graded question bank.

Q1. A report says “iron = 4.2”. Give four pieces of information needed before this is an interpretable analytical result.






Hint Q1





Name the chemical quantity, material, unit and relevant preparation conditions.









Answer Q1





Specify which iron quantity (for example dissolved iron after a defined reduction), the sampled material and scope, the unit and concentration or amount basis, and the preparation/measurement conditions. “Iron” alone does not distinguish original Fe(II), dissolved total iron and particulate material; 4.2 alone has no unit or denominator.





Q2. A homogeneous solution is 12.0 mg chloride/L. How much chloride is in 400 mL? What is its concentration in g/L?






Hint Q2





Use litres for amount; use the mg-to-g conversion separately for concentration.









Answer Q2





\(m=12.0\times0.400=4.80\) mg. Concentration is \(12.0/1000=0.0120\) g/L. Taking a portion does not change a homogeneous solution’s concentration; amount and concentration have different meanings.





Q3. A 2.00 mL aliquot is made to 20.00 mL total and measured as 0.300 mg/L. What was the original concentration?






Hint Q3





Reverse the final-to-aliquot volume factor.









Answer Q3





The factor is \(20.00/2.00=10\), so original concentration is 3.00 mg/L, conditional on no analyte loss or addition. Adding 20 mL solvent would produce a different final volume from making up to 20 mL.





Q4. Why is “mg/L = ppm” not a universal unit definition?






Hint Q4





Compare a mass-per-volume quantity with a mass fraction.









Answer Q4





mg/L has a volume denominator; a mass fraction needs a mass denominator. For a sufficiently dilute water solution they can be approximately related through density, but this is an assumption, not a definition that applies to every material.





Q5. Two flasks have the same calibrated final concentration. Can their original samples have different concentrations?






Hint Q5





Ask whether the preparation factors are equal.









Answer Q5





Yes. A final concentration of 1 mg/L after factors 5 and 20 corresponds to original values 5 and 20 mg/L respectively, if the preparation model is valid. A signal cannot replace the aliquot and total-volume record.





Q6. A table has four inlet rows followed by four outlet rows. Can row 1 be paired with row 5 for a before/after analysis?






Hint Q6





A pair is defined by experimental identity, not by table order.









Answer Q6





No paired design is supplied by those positions. A subject/sample identifier and the collection design must establish which observations are genuinely matched. Arbitrary row pairing invents evidence.





Q7. The concentration field is missing for an unsuccessful measurement. Is replacing it with zero a harmless way to calculate a mean?






Hint Q7





Distinguish absent measurement evidence from an observed zero.









Answer Q7





No. Zero is a numerical result; missing means the quantity was not established. Replacing missing values with zero can bias the mean. Document the failure and report how many valid results support a summary.





Q8. A report renders perfectly from a new R session. Does that prove its chemical conclusion?






Hint Q8





Which kinds of mistakes can be repeated exactly?









Answer Q8





It establishes useful computational reproducibility, but can repeat a wrong unit, unrepresentative sampling, incorrect preparation factor or nonspecific response. The chemical model and evidence still need review.

title: Exercise: error and uncertainty
text:
Background
Repeated readings of one stable preparation can reveal reading repeatability. They do not by themselves reveal sampling, extraction loss, stock uncertainty or shared volume effects. For independent normal readings, \(s/\sqrt n\) estimates the reading contribution to uncertainty in their mean. Standard uncertainty is on an SD-like scale; it is not automatically a 95% half-width.
For \(c=c_sV_a/V_f\) and small independent input uncertainties,
\[u(c)=c\sqrt{[u(c_s)/c_s]^2+[u(V_a)/V_a]^2+[u(V_f)/V_f]^2}.\]
Correlated inputs require covariance terms. A known significant bias calls for investigation or a justified correction with its uncertainty, rather than an arbitrary extra error bar.

title: Exercise: error and uncertainty
text:
By hand
B1. A reference is 10.00 mg/L. Method A has mean 10.00 and SD 0.02 mg/L; B has mean 10.50 and the same SD. Compare precision and estimated bias. Here reference uncertainty is neglected. Hint

B3. A 100.0 mg/L stock has standard uncertainty 0.4 mg/L. A 5.000 mL aliquot has standard uncertainty 0.006 mL; final volume 50.00 mL has standard uncertainty 0.03 mL. Calculate final concentration, each output-scale contribution and their combined standard uncertainty. Hint
B4. Reading noise contributes \(0.20/\sqrt n\) mg/L and an independent shared component is 0.10 mg/L. Find combined uncertainty at \(n=1\) and \(n=100\), and its limit as n grows. Hint
B5. A report gives “10.00 ± 0.04 mg/L” without defining ±. Name two possible meanings and the information needed to distinguish them. Hint

title: Exercise: error and uncertainty
text:
Hints






Hint B1





Precision concerns repeated values; estimated bias compares mean with a suitable reference. They answer different questions.









Hint B2





Divide SD by \(\sqrt5\) for the reading contribution to the mean. The individual reading distribution retains its own spread.









Hint B3





Final concentration is 10 mg/L. Convert each relative input uncertainty to an output-scale contribution before adding its square.









Hint B4





Combine the squared reading and shared components. Only the independent reading term is divided by n.









Hint B5





It could denote a standard uncertainty, expanded uncertainty with a stated coverage factor, or a confidence-interval half-width under a sampling model.









Hints E1–E4





Track reading noise, common random offset and deliberately known fixed bias separately. The bias correction is exact only by this toy model’s assumption; real corrections can have their own uncertainty.









Hint R1





Compare both bias_mg_l and sd_mg_l. A single accidentally close mean is not full validation.









Hint R2





Change only the stock contribution from 0.040 to 0.020 mg/L. Keep the two volume contributions.









Hint R3





sqrt() is applied to the sum of variances. A known uncorrected bias is not being treated as an extra random term in this illustrative curve.









Hint R4





sd() describes spread among readings. The supplied uncertainty includes a component shared by those readings, which their scatter cannot estimate.

title: Exercise: error and uncertainty
text:
Solutions






Solutions B1–B5





B1. A and B have equal repeat precision under the stated conditions. A has estimated bias zero in this series; B has +0.50 mg/L. Equal precision does not imply equal closeness to the reference, and this neglects reference uncertainty only for the example.
B2. \(u_{reading}(\bar x)=0.3162/\sqrt5\approx0.1414\) mg/L. Individual readings retain SD 0.3162 mg/L; the mean has a smaller reading component. Neither number establishes sampling, recovery or common-bias uncertainty.
B3. \(c=100(5/50)=10\) mg/L. Contributions are 0.040, 0.012 and 0.006 mg/L. Their squared sum is 0.001780 (mg/L)², so \(u(c)=0.04219\) mg/L. The calculation assumes a valid model, small uncertainties and independent inputs.
B4. At n=1, \(u=\sqrt{0.20^2+0.10^2}=0.22361\) mg/L. At n=100, \(u=\sqrt{0.20^2/100+0.10^2}=0.10198\) mg/L. It approaches 0.10 mg/L, because repeated readings do not create new information about the common effect.
B5. If 0.04 is a standard uncertainty, no 95% coverage is implied by itself. If it is expanded uncertainty, give k and its coverage rationale. If it is a confidence-interval half-width, give the sampling/model construction and level. Without that information the reader cannot interpret the uncertainty claim.









Solutions E1–E4





E1. The reading-only component is 0.20, 0.06325 and 0.0200 mg/L at n=1,10,100; combined values are about 0.22361, 0.11832 and 0.10198 mg/L. The mean can remain displaced because bias and the common offset do not shrink within the run.
E2. The readings coincide and their observed SD is zero for n≥2. The known bias and realised shared offset remain. Zero observed repeatability scatter therefore does not establish an exact analytical result.
E3. Subtracting the specified known bias removes the fixed 0.30 mg/L effect. The common random offset remains, along with residual reading noise. The model assumes the correction exact; a real correction may add an uncertainty component.
E4. A new run draws a new common offset. Many readings within one preparation retain the same offset. Studying independent preparations can reveal sources that within-solution repeatability cannot, provided the design actually varies the relevant steps.









Solutions R1–R4





R1. B is precise but displaced. A/B both have SD about 0.01581 mg/L; C has SD 0.31623 mg/L. C’s mean is 10.00 in this small series, but that does not prove unbiased performance in different samples, matrices or conditions.
R2. New combined uncertainty is \(\sqrt{0.020^2+0.012^2+0.006^2}=0.02408\) mg/L. The unchanged volume terms prevent a simple factor-of-two change.
R3. The shared 0.10 mg/L component remains. The curve omits a known uncorrected bias rather than pretending it is random; that bias requires its own investigation or justified correction. The values are standard uncertainties, not 95% interval half-widths.
R4. R’s SD measures within-run reading spread and may differ from the supplied population reading SD in a finite sample. The model uncertainty concerns the mean and combines a shrinking independent reading contribution with a shared component. Changing a common offset moves all readings together without widening their scatter. At n=1, sample SD is undefined, not evidence of no variability.

title: Exercise: error and uncertainty
text:
Where this leads
Calibration and quality control adds uncertain slope and intercept when a response is converted to concentration. Ask which uncertainty components and validity checks accompany every later reported result.

title: Quiz: error and uncertainty
text:
Try each question before opening its hint or answer. These practice questions check chemical reasoning and small calculations; they are not a graded question bank.

Q1. Method A gives repeated values near 10.0 mg/L with SD 0.30; B gives values near 10.5 with SD 0.02. The reference is 10.0. Which is more precise, and which shows a positive mean difference?






Hint Q1





Treat spread and reference difference as separate properties.









Answer Q1





B is more precise under these repeat conditions but has an observed positive difference of about 0.5 mg/L from the reference. Good repeatability is not the same as low bias. A rigorous bias assessment would also consider reference uncertainty and design.





Q2. Nine independent stable readings have sample SD 0.30 mg/L. What is the reading contribution to uncertainty in their mean?






Hint Q2





Use \(s/\sqrt n\) for this specific contribution.









Answer Q2





\(0.30/\sqrt9=0.10\) mg/L. Individual readings still have spread about 0.30 mg/L. The smaller mean uncertainty does not include any shared stock, preparation or sampling component.





Q3. A mean has an independent reading contribution 0.03 mg/L and a shared component 0.04 mg/L. Find combined standard uncertainty.






Hint Q3





Add squared independent contributions, then take the square root.









Answer Q3





\(u=\sqrt{0.03^2+0.04^2}=0.05\) mg/L. This is a standard uncertainty, not automatically a 95% interval or a complete method budget.





Q4. What happens to the previous combined uncertainty if indefinitely many independent readings drive the reading component towards zero?






Hint Q4





Which component is shared by the readings?









Answer Q4





It approaches 0.04 mg/L, not zero. More readings of the same solution do not independently re-establish the shared component.





Q5. Every reading has the same known +0.20 mg/L bias. Will increasing n remove it?






Hint Q5





A fixed common displacement is not independent zero-mean noise.









Answer Q5





No. The mean retains the fixed bias. Investigate or use an appropriately justified correction with its uncertainty. An arbitrary larger or smaller error bar does not itself correct the result.





Q6. Two volume uncertainties arise partly from the same temperature error. Can they always be combined as independent squared terms?






Hint Q6





Shared causes can induce covariance.









Answer Q6





No. Covariance terms can matter. The independent-input square-sum formula is conditional on independence; the signs of model sensitivities and the correlations determine how shared effects propagate.





Q7. A preparation has repeated identical displayed readings, so its observed SD is zero. Is the method uncertainty zero?






Hint Q7





Which sources can move every reading together without changing their scatter?









Answer Q7





No. Common calibration, preparation, recovery, display resolution and sampling effects can remain. Repeating one prepared solution does not reveal every relevant source, and zero displayed scatter is not a validation of exactness.





Q8. A result is reported with standard uncertainty 0.05 mg/L. Can the reader interpret ±0.05 as a 95% interval?






Hint Q8





A coverage interpretation needs a construction and assumptions.









Answer Q8





Not from that statement alone. Standard uncertainty is on an SD-like scale. Expanded uncertainty needs a stated coverage factor and rationale; a confidence interval needs a sampling/model construction and level. State which quantity and components are included.

What relation turns signal into concentration?

Known final concentrations give measured responses.

Fit the measured response direction

A=a+bc+e.

Slope ≈ 0.198799 L/mg Fe.

Retain the estimated intercept

Intercept ≈ 0.003874.

A nonzero offset does not prove a particular cause. Do not force zero or blank-subtract an already blank-referenced response again.

Bracket the intended measurement range

These standards cover 0–4 mg Fe/L final.

Residuals are observations minus fitted responses

What pattern would challenge a straight line?

Curvature, changing spread or an unusual observation. Ask before revealing the faulty comparison dataset.

A high R² can hide systematic error

The second dataset is deliberately curved.

title: Calibration and quality control
text:
Investigate before excluding a standard

A point is not wrong merely because it worsens the fit.

Check preparation, transcription, instrument response and protocol. Exclusion needs evidence and a recorded reason.

A narrower range needs evidence

Which standards and checks would validate the proposed range?

Do not remove upper points solely to improve appearance. Model and range selection must fit the analytical purpose.

Changing variance is another model concern

Ordinary least squares assumes the specified response-error structure.

If variance grows with concentration, weighting may be appropriate but requires a justified variance model. Recognising the limitation is core; advanced weighted fitting is optional.

\hat c=(\bar A-a)/b.

A concentration estimate is not the original sample result

The current unit is mg Fe/L in the final coloured solution.

section: Three materials ask different QC questions

Three materials ask different QC questions

Which would reveal introduced contamination?

A method blank. Then ask which checks calibration under independent known concentration and which probes incremental sample response.

title: Calibration and quality control
section: Independence matters for a check standard
text:
Independence matters for a check standard

The same wrong stock can make standards and checks agree.

An independently sourced material can challenge a shared preparation error. Matching matrix and measurand still matter.

title: Calibration and quality control
text:
Acceptance criteria precede the results
What action follows a failure?

Use a documented rule established for the intended procedure. Recalibration, investigation, remeasurement or withholding should follow evidence, not a desire to retain results.

title: Calibration and quality control
section: A weak signal can be detectable but poorly quantified
text:
A weak signal can be detectable but poorly quantified

Distinguishing a signal from blanks is a different requirement from precise quantification.

Do not use below-limit as a synonym for zero. Decision probabilities, uncertainty and method conditions matter.

section: Estimate blank variation from independent blanks
text:
Estimate blank variation from independent blanks

Mean = 0.0100; SD = 0.001348 signal units.

The twelve method blanks belong to a separate ideal low-level example. Repeated readings of one blank do not measure all blank-preparation variation.

title: Calibration and quality control

Keep a heuristic in its proper role

3s_{blank}/b=0.02023 mg/L; 10s_{blank}/b=0.06742 mg/L.

Sensitivity is 0.200 in this separate example. These are illustrative concentration increments, not universally validated LOD and LOQ values.

title: Calibration and quality control

text:
A signal threshold includes the blank level

Threshold here: mean blank plus three SD.

Do not confuse the response threshold with a blank-relative concentration increment or subtract a blank twice.

title: Calibration and quality control
text:
Uncertainty remains after calibration inversion

Reading noise and uncertain slope/intercept both contribute.

Use the supplied inverse helper, which propagates coefficient covariance. A forward response prediction interval is not a concentration interval.

Final concentration ≈ 2.3981 mg Fe/L; approximate 95% interval 2.3886–2.4077.

The interval excludes sample preparation, volumes, sampling and matrix/recovery bias. Ask what must be added before interpreting it as a complete original-sample uncertainty.

Outside range; failed independent check; below quantification requirement.

Outside range needs appropriate new measurement; failed check requires investigation and withheld affected results; weak response needs an appropriate qualified report rather than a manufactured zero.

title: Exercise: equilibrium and titration
text:
Background
For the strong-acid reaction \(\mathrm{H^++OH^-\rightarrow H_2O}\), equivalence means equal reacted amounts. With 1:1 stoichiometry, \(c_a=c_bV_{eq}/V_a\). Read delivered burette volume as final minus initial, then subtract justified blank consumption on the same volume basis. A measured endpoint estimates \(V_{eq}\) under a stated indicator or numerical rule.
At 25 °C the ideal strong-acid/strong-base equivalence has pH 7. A weak acid’s conjugate base changes equivalence pH without changing the number of moles that must be neutralised. The supplied weak-acid comparison uses pKa 4.76.
For this simplified hardness procedure assume accessible Ca and Mg react selectively 1:1 with EDTA under the supplied conditions. Report the combined amount as CaCO₃ using 100.09 g/mol. This equivalent basis does not prove that carbonate was present or distinguish Ca from Mg. All course data are simulated.

title: Exercise: equilibrium and titration
text:
By hand
B1. A 25.00 mL strong-acid aliquot reaches its estimated endpoint after 25.00 mL of standardised 0.1000 mol/L base. Calculate acid concentration and reacted amount. Show where litres are necessary. Hint
B2. The same initial amount is instead a weak monoprotic acid. Does its equivalence require less base? Must equivalence still occur at pH 7? Explain using stoichiometry and equilibrium separately. Hint

In R
Open the supplied project at its root. The following workflow runs in a fresh R session and does not require a demo export. It uses your earlier read_csv, mutate and plotting skills, adding diff() for consecutive changes.
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
curve <- read_csv("data/course/acid-titration.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
slopes <- data.frame(
  midpoint_ml = (head(curve$volume_ml, -1) + tail(curve$volume_ml, -1)) / 2,
  ph_per_ml = diff(curve$ph) / diff(curve$volume_ml))
ggplot(curve, aes(volume_ml, ph)) + geom_line() +
  labs(x = "0.1000 mol/L base added (mL)", y = "pH") + theme_minimal()
ggplot(slopes, aes(midpoint_ml, ph_per_ml)) + geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Addition midpoint (mL)", y = "Finite-difference pH per mL") +
  theme_minimal()
acid_mol_l <- 0.1000 * 25.00 / 25.00
hardness <- read_csv("data/course/edta.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(delivered_ml = final_burette_ml - initial_burette_ml,
         corrected_ml = delivered_ml - blank_ml,
         moles_metal = edta_mol_l * corrected_ml / 1000,
         hardness_mg_l_CaCO3 = moles_metal * 100.09 * 1000 / (sample_ml / 1000))
hardness
write_csv(hardness, "output/titration-exercise.csv")
R1. Explain the units in each calculated column. Locate the steep region and explain why the slope maximum is an exploratory check rather than complete endpoint validation. Hint
R2. Compare H1a, H1b and H2a. Which are independent preparations of the same supplied sample, and which values may be described as separate waters? State one source of uncertainty not estimated by their difference. Hint

title: Exercise: equilibrium and titration
text:
Hints






B1: amount before concentration





Use \(n=cV\) with volume in litres, then divide by the original acid volume. Matching millilitre units may cancel only when you use a volume ratio.









B2: two different questions





Stoichiometry determines the amount of titrant; equilibrium determines species and pH. A conjugate base remains after neutralising a weak acid.









B3: delivered volume and reporting basis





First subtract initial from final, then the matched blank. EDTA mol equals accessible metal mol in this scenario. Convert to equivalent CaCO₃ mass and divide by the original sample volume.









B4: use actual spacing





Divide 2.0 pH units by the difference in millilitres. The midpoint is the mean of the two added volumes.









E1: compare volume and pH separately





Read both equivalence outputs before inspecting the chosen endpoint. The initial acid amount is held fixed by the model.









E2: dilute titrant, fixed moles





Halving titrant concentration requires twice its volume for the same moles.









E3: endpoint bias is not reading precision





Compare the amount inferred at the trigger with the known model amount. The simulation excludes noise, incomplete mixing and instrument/junction effects.









R1: read diff





diff gives consecutive differences. Unequal volume steps require their own denominators; differentiation amplifies noise.









R2: inspect sample_id





Preparation IDs are not the same as independent collection IDs. Titrant standardisation or endpoint bias can be common to several preparations.









R3: reuse the model with a new denominator





The corrected volume is 4.00 mL, but this aliquot is 25.00 mL rather than 50.00 mL.

title: Exercise: equilibrium and titration
text:
Solutions






Full worked solutions





B1. Base amount is \(0.1000\times0.02500=0.002500\) mol. The 1:1 reaction therefore consumed 0.002500 mol acid. Dividing by 0.02500 L acid gives 0.1000 mol/L. Multiplying concentration by 25.00 without converting mL to L would be a thousand-fold amount error.
B2. With the same monoprotic acid amount, the same base moles are required, so equivalence volume remains 25.00 mL at the same base concentration. A weak acid leaves its conjugate base at equivalence, and its pH can exceed 7. Acid strength changes the pH curve, not the supplied number of acid moles.
B3. Delivered volume \(6.30-0.10=6.20\) mL; corrected volume \(6.20-0.05=6.15\) mL. Metal amount is \(0.01000\times0.00615=6.15\times10^{-5}\) mol. Equivalent CaCO₃ mass is \(6.15\times10^{-5}\times100.09\times1000=6.155535\) mg. Divide by 0.05000 L to obtain 123.1107 mg/L as CaCO₃. Omitting positive blank consumption biases this estimate high. It is not a separate calcium result.
B4. \((8.0-6.0)/(25.10-24.90)=10.0\) pH units per mL, assigned to 25.00 mL. The denominator represents actual added volume. A difference per row silently assumes equal step sizes and can distort the inferred steep region.
E1. Equivalence volume stays fixed while weak-acid equivalence pH rises. The pH 7 trigger is reached before weak-acid equivalence and underestimates the acid amount in this model. No general rule sets every endpoint to pH 7.
E2. Required base moles remain 2.500 mmol. At 0.0500 mol/L, equivalence volume is \(0.002500/0.0500=0.05000\) L = 50.00 mL for either acid model. The changed base concentration, not acid strength, caused the volume change.
E3. A trigger below equivalence pH usually stops early and gives low inferred acid; one above it stops late and gives high inferred acid. The precise volume depends on pKa and trigger. This is a systematic endpoint-rule problem, not a lack of printed precision. If the selected trigger is already outside the displayed titration range, it is unavailable rather than evidence of zero acid. The ideal model does not supply real electrode, volume, mixing or recovery uncertainty.
R1. Delivered/corrected volumes are mL, metal amount mol, hardness mg/L as CaCO₃. The slope plot locates a steep region near 25 mL; its value depends on step sizes and noise. A validated endpoint method must address these effects.
R2. H1a/H1b are separate preparations of H1, giving 123.1107 and 124.1116 mg/L as CaCO₃. H2a is another supplied sample at 191.1719 mg/L. Two preparations of one water do not become two independently collected waters. Shared titrant concentration uncertainty or endpoint bias is not established from their difference.
R3. The corrected consumption is 0.00400 L; amount is \(4.00\times10^{-5}\) mol, equivalent to 4.0036 mg CaCO₃ in 0.02500 L. Result is 160.144 mg/L as CaCO₃:
new_hardness <- 0.01000 * ((4.10 - 0.10) / 1000) *
                  100.09 * 1000 / (25.00 / 1000)
new_hardness

Where this leads
Potentiometry explains electrode signals and their calibration. The titration’s concentration and volume uncertainties return in later reporting problems. Practice quiz checks the chemical reasoning.

title: Quiz: equilibrium and titration
text:
Try each question before opening its hint. Then explain the answer in chemical and measurement terms. Lecture · Exercise.

Q1. Two monoprotic acids have the same initial amount, but one is weak. With the same standardised base, must the weaker acid have a smaller equivalence volume?






Hint





Keep the reaction coefficients separate from the equilibrium pH.









Answer





No. Both require the same number of base moles for 1:1 neutralisation, so their equivalence volumes are equal at fixed titrant concentration. Their pH curves and suitable indicators can differ.




Q2. A 20.00 mL acid aliquot requires 15.00 mL of 0.08000 mol/L base at its estimated endpoint. Calculate the acid concentration under the 1:1 model.






Hint





Use base amount, then original sample volume.









Answer





\(n_b=0.08000\times0.01500=0.001200\) mol. Dividing by 0.02000 L gives 0.06000 mol/L acid. Endpoint validity and standardisation uncertainty remain assumptions.




Q3. A 20.00 mL water sample uses 0.01000 mol/L EDTA. Initial/final burette readings are 0.20/4.25 mL and the matched blank consumes 0.05 mL. What is hardness as CaCO₃?






Hint





Delivered volume is final minus initial; then subtract the blank. Use 100.09 g/mol.









Answer





Corrected consumption is \(4.25-0.20-0.05=4.00\) mL. This is \(4.00\times10^{-5}\) mol, equivalent to 4.0036 mg CaCO₃ in 0.02000 L: 200.18 mg/L as CaCO₃. It does not identify calcium and magnesium separately.




Q4. The next pH measurement is made after a 0.10 mL step rather than the previous 1.00 mL step. Is a raw pH change per row a comparable slope?






Hint





What unit should a derivative have?









Answer





No. Divide each pH difference by its actual volume difference to obtain pH per mL, and assign it to the interval midpoint. Different step sizes distort changes per row. Differencing also magnifies noise.




Q5. A program always stops a titration at pH 7. A weak-acid equivalence is above pH 7. What error direction is expected for the inferred acid amount in this ideal increasing curve?






Hint





A lower trigger is reached before equivalence.









Answer





It stops early, so titrant amount and inferred acid amount are biased low. Printing more endpoint digits does not correct an inappropriate endpoint rule.




Q6. An EDTA result is reported as 120 mg/L as CaCO₃. Has the analyst demonstrated dissolved carbonate at 120 mg/L?






Hint





A reporting equivalent is not an identification result.









Answer





No. The result expresses the counted accessible metal equivalents on the CaCO₃ molar-mass basis under the assumed selective procedure. It neither establishes carbonate presence nor separates individual metal concentrations.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
About this lecture

Explain why the complete cell and activity conditions matter.
Fit and invert a logarithmic fluoride calibration in R.
Separate a shared drift failure from sample-specific matrix mismatch.


The exercise begins with pen-and-paper tasks, then embeds the exploratory model and finishes in R using the existing course datasets. Keep each numerical result connected to its chemical quantity. All data and profiles are simulated; the demonstrations do not validate actual instruments or preparation methods.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
section: A voltage belongs to a cell
text:
A voltage belongs to a cell

Which two functions are required?

Indicator and reference electrodes. A combined electrode packages both functions; it does not remove the reference.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
section: The indicator responds; the reference anchors
text:
The indicator responds; the reference anchors

The measured potential also includes the reference and junction.

Changes in either can affect the reading. A voltage is not an intrinsic concentration label.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
Why use a high-input-impedance meter?

Read potential with negligible net measurement current.

Contrast with deliberately current-measuring electrochemical methods. Do not imply a potentiometric electrode is a current detector.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
Activity gives the thermodynamic response

a_i=\gamma_i c_i/c^\circ.

Activity is dimensionless. A concentration calibration transfers only when the activity relationship is appropriate to standards and sample.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
Write the logarithmic relationship
E=K+(2.303RT/zF)\log_{10} a_i.

The sign here includes signed ion charge and the chosen potential convention. At twenty-five Celsius the monovalent magnitude is about 59.16 mV per decade.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
section: Anion and cation slopes need a convention
text:
Anion and cation slopes need a convention

For this fluoride example, increasing concentration lowers the potential.

Do not infer a chemistry error solely from a sign without checking instrument polarity and cell convention.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
Match conditions before using concentration

Ionic-strength adjustment helps; it does not remove every interference.

Discuss activity coefficients, complexes and junction changes. The electrode can respond to free species rather than total element.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
pH is already logarithmic

pH=-\log_{10}a_{H^+}.

One pH unit is a tenfold activity change. Avoid treating pH itself as an ordinary concentration in mol/L.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
Buffers establish the pH calibration

Use appropriate buffers and measurement temperature.

The illustrated ideal intercept is not universal. The cell and calibration establish the actual response.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
Inspect the fluoride standards

Range here: 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻³ mol/L at matched conditions.

This is the supplied scenario range, not a universal electrode range or a full validation.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
Transform the explanatory quantity
mutate(log_c = log10(fluoride_mol_l))

Numerically this takes concentration in mol/L relative to one mol/L. Zero and negative concentrations cannot be ordinary log-calibration points.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
section: The correct axes reveal the model
text:
The correct axes reveal the model

The same observations are nearly linear against log concentration.

Ask why a straight line on the untransformed concentration axis would be inappropriate.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
Read the slope per decade

Fitted slope = −59.10 mV per decade.

A factor of ten in concentration is a one-unit change on the explanatory axis. The fitted intercept is about minus 97.42 mV.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
Invert in two steps
First (E-a)/b; then c=10^{(E-a)/b} mol/L.

For the measured 121.2 mV, the exponent is about minus 3.699. Forgetting the power of ten leaves a log value rather than concentration.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
Report the accepted early sample

121.2 mV → 2.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol/L.

Check that this lies within the supplied calibration range. Identity and matrix compatibility remain assumptions.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
section: Check the calibration at a known concentration
text:
Check the calibration at a known concentration

The check is 1.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol/L; exercise tolerance ±2.0 mV.

The expected response is 138.98 mV. The check is separate from merely asking whether the fit is straight.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
The early block passes

Observed 139.1 mV; error +0.12 mV.

Use the preselected rule. Do not re-estimate a tolerance after observing the data.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
The later block fails

Observed 145.0 mV; error +6.02 mV.

Withhold the affected later sample. Investigate, establish satisfactory calibration and checks, then remeasure.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
section: A drift does not identify its cause
text:
A drift does not identify its cause

Conditioning, junction, temperature and matrix changes are candidates.

The graph alone does not establish which occurred. Avoid automatically subtracting the observed check error from every later sample.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
section: Uncertainty changes shape through the inverse
text:
Uncertainty changes shape through the inverse

Symmetric voltage limits can become asymmetric concentration limits.

Exponentiation maps additive voltage uncertainty into multiplicative concentration uncertainty. Never attach a voltage SD directly to a concentration result.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
Place other electrochemical signals
Potential: potentiometry. Current: amperometry or voltammetry. Charge: coulometry.

Different signals need different measurement models. Coulometric amount additionally requires the intended reaction to account for the charge.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
Transfer: a 17.8 mV decrease

Predict the concentration factor before calculating.

With slope minus 59.10, factor is about 2.001. The accepted estimate becomes about four times ten to minus four mol/L.

title: Electrodes and potentiometry
text:
Would this measure total fluorine?

Free-ion response does not automatically include every chemical form.

Ask what preparation and speciation evidence would be needed. Return to the measurand rather than treating the instrument name as the answer.
