title: Exercise: UV and visible absorption
text: Connect an absorbing chemical species to a defensible iron concentration. Retrieve plotting and regression in R; extend these with keyed preparation joins and inverse-calibration uncertainty.

title: Exercise: UV and visible absorption
text:
Background
How much dissolved iron is in the supplied filtered water, and which results are supported by the measurements? We will make a coloured iron complex, use its light absorption to estimate concentration, then check the preparation factor, calibration, and independent quality-control result.
Use your familiar R project, CSV, plotting, and straight-line skills. The new steps are matching preparation records by ID and accounting for uncertainty when converting a signal to concentration.
Download the complete project, extract it, and open analyticalchem.Rproj. Keep report.Rmd at the project root. The project needs R packages readr, dplyr, ggplot2, knitr, and rmarkdown. See the R reference for package setup.
All measurements here are simulated. This is an analysis exercise; use an approved practical protocol for any actual laboratory work.

Make an absorber we can measure
Iron(II) reacts with 1,10-phenanthroline, abbreviated phen, to form a red-orange complex:
\[\mathrm{Fe^{2+} + 3\,phen \rightleftharpoons [Fe(phen)_3]^{2+}}\]
Three bidentate ligands coordinate one iron ion. We measure the complex near 510 nm. Reduction maintains the iron(II) state; controlled acidity and excess ligand support colour formation. University laboratory background



One Fe²⁺ combines with three phen ligands. Boxes describe stoichiometry, not molecular geometry.


For this exercise, assume quantitative reduction and complex formation and no iron loss. The measurand is mg Fe/L in the supplied filtered water, including iron converted to Fe(II) in the assumed preparation. It is not the original Fe(II) concentration before treatment. No evidence about particulate iron or digestion recovery is supplied.
Predict: if reduction is incomplete, will the result be biased high or low? Explain using the species that absorbs the light.


Connect the apparatus to absorbance
At a selected wavelength, light passes through a cuvette. The detector measures transmitted intensity \(I\) relative to reference intensity \(I_0\):
\[T = I/I_0, \qquad A = -\log_{10}(T)\]
A reagent blank contains the preparation reagents without the analyte and accounts for their background under matched conditions. Absorbance in these files is already referenced to a reagent blank. Do not blank-correct it again.



Selected light crosses a 1.00 cm path; the detector measures transmitted light.


A transmittance of 0.50 corresponds to absorbance 0.301. If twice as much analyte doubles absorbance within the linear range, it does not halve transmittance: \(T=10^{-A}\).
For an appropriate dilute solution at fixed wavelength and path length, Beer–Lambert behaviour is \(A=\varepsilon l c\), with \(c\) in mol/L when using a molar absorptivity. Here our calibration uses mg of elemental Fe/L, so its slope has units L/mg Fe. Do not substitute that slope into a molar equation without converting the concentration basis.

title: Exercise: UV and visible absorption
text:
By hand
B1. Convert transmittance 0.50 into absorbance. What transmittance follows if absorbance doubles? To test whether halving transmission is a general rule, repeat the reasoning for transmittance 0.80. Hint
B2. A line is \(A=0.004+0.199c\). An unknown gives \(A=0.4806\). Estimate final concentration and the original concentration for 10.00 mL made up to 50.00 mL. State the concentration basis. Hint
B3. A later independent check recovers 85.2% against an exercise acceptance window of 95–105%. Can an in-range sample from that block be reported? Hint
B4. A separate ideal absorber has supplied molar absorptivity \(\varepsilon=2000\) L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹ and path 1.00 cm. If absorbance is 0.600, calculate molar concentration. Why must the iron calibration slope in L/mg Fe not be substituted numerically for this molar absorptivity? Hint

title: Exercise: UV and visible absorption
text:
Explore
Predict first; change one setting at a time. This model isolates optical effects; it does not simulate a complete validated method.



E1. Reset the demo so stray light is zero and wavelength is 510 nm. Double path length from 1.00 to 2.00 cm with recalibration on. Explain changes in absorbance, transmission and inverse concentration. Repeat with recalibration off, distinguishing the algebraic candidate from a reportable result. Hint
E2. Reset again. Move wavelength from 510 to 450 nm while retaining recalibration and zero stray light. Which quantities change, and which remain the same in the matched model? Hint
E3. From reset, add stray light and inspect both response and standard residual plots. Does refitting a straight line remove the underlying curvature? Distinguish a nonzero residual from failure of the supplied 0.005-absorbance exercise check. Export a scenario; move its CSV into your project output/ folder and reproduce the standard residual plot in R. Hint

title: Exercise: UV and visible absorption
text:
In R

R1. Choose the wavelength from a spectrum
Plot both traces. Explain the proposed wavelength and what one row represents. Hint
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
spectra <- read_csv("data/spectra.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
ggplot(spectra, aes(wavelength_nm, absorbance, colour = trace)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Wavelength (nm)", y = "Absorbance", colour = "Solution") +
  theme_minimal()



The illustrative standard has a maximum near 510 nm; the reagent blank is small.


The spectral shape supports choosing 510 nm for a strong response. A maximum also makes a small wavelength-setting error less consequential than on a steep spectral flank. It does not prove that other sample components cannot absorb. This simulated envelope is not a reference spectrum for identifying a compound.
Each row is a wavelength in one scan. These rows do not give hundreds of independently prepared standards.


R2. Fit the familiar calibration
Interpret slope and intercept with units and inspect the residual pattern. State what this diagnostic cannot establish about a sample matrix. Hint
standards <- read_csv("data/standards.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
fit <- lm(absorbance ~ standard_mg_l, data = standards)
coef(fit)
a <- unname(coef(fit)[1])
b <- unname(coef(fit)[2])
ggplot(standards, aes(standard_mg_l, absorbance)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_abline(intercept = a, slope = b) +
  labs(x = "Iron in final solution (mg Fe/L)",
       y = "Absorbance at 510 nm") +
  theme_minimal()



Eighteen simulated calibration solutions cover 0–4 mg Fe/L.


The fitted relationship is approximately \(A=0.003874+0.198799c\). The nonzero intercept is estimated, not forced to zero. Its existence alone does not identify the source of the offset.
The concentration is deliberately set; absorbance is the response. Fitting standard_mg_l ~ absorbance describes a different regression. Estimate an unknown using the inverse of our fitted response model:
\[\hat c_{final} = (\bar A_{unknown}-a)/b\]
standards <- standards |> mutate(residual = residuals(fit))
ggplot(standards, aes(standard_mg_l, residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Iron in final solution (mg Fe/L)",
       y = "Observed minus fitted absorbance") +
  theme_minimal()



Residuals reveal departures from the line, not whether the sample matrix is compatible.


Look for curvature, changing spread, and unusual observations. Small residuals on standards cannot establish recovery or selectivity in an unknown water. Do not remove a point simply to improve the fit.


R3. Match the measurement to its preparation
Check key uniqueness and matches, then explain why the deliberately reversed preparation-table order must not affect the join. Hint
P01 and P02 are separate preparations of W1, each read three times. We will first analyse P01. P03 and P04 belong to W2; P04 is a newly measured preparation with a smaller aliquot. P05 belongs to a later measurement block.



W1 is one supplied water sample with two preparations and three readings per preparation.


readings <- read_csv("data/readings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
preparations <- read_csv("data/preparations.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(preparations$preparation_id),
          all(readings$preparation_id %in% preparations$preparation_id))
means <- readings |>
  group_by(preparation_id) |>
  summarise(m = n(), mean_absorbance = mean(absorbance),
            .groups = "drop")
joined <- means |> left_join(preparations, by = "preparation_id")
joined
left_join() attaches the matching preparation information to each measurement summary using the ID. It does not assume that the files have the same row order. The checks require one preparation record per key and a match for every measured preparation. Inspect IDs, row count, units, and missing values after joining.
For P01, mean absorbance is 0.480620, corresponding to about 2.398 mg Fe/L in the final coloured solution.


R4. Return to the original water concentration
Calculate P01 on the original-water basis and explain which volume the correction uses. Hint



A 10.00 mL aliquot is made up to 50.00 mL total, including all reagents and solvent.


\[\hat c_{original}=\hat c_{final}\frac{V_{final}}{V_{aliquot}}\]
For P01, \(V_{final}=50.00\) mL and \(V_{aliquot}=10.00\) mL. Multiply by 5, giving about 11.99 mg Fe/L in the supplied water. The final volume is the total volume, not the amount of water added.
Predict: P04 uses 5.00 mL made up to 50.00 mL. Should its final concentration be multiplied by 5 or 10? Which recorded field tells you?


R5. Check range before reporting a number
Identify the unsupported old preparation and distinguish it from the newly measured dilution. Hint
For this exercise, require every repeated reading to lie between the fitted responses at the lowest and highest calibration concentrations. This is a supplied working-range rule, not a general validation of the method.
response_limits <- predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(standard_mg_l = c(0, 4)))
range_check <- readings |>
  group_by(preparation_id) |>
  summarise(in_range = all(absorbance >= response_limits[1] &
                          absorbance <= response_limits[2]), .groups = "drop")
range_check



P03 exceeds the calibrated response range; P04 is a newly measured dilution within range.


P03 is outside range. Its old signal cannot be rescued by changing a dilution factor in the table. P04 is a new measurement of a new aliquot: its mean absorbance is 0.540610 and its dilution factor is 10. This gives about 27.00 mg Fe/L for W2 under the stated assumptions.


R6. Use an independent quality-control check
Apply the stated block checks and export only supported concentration estimates, retaining identifiers and reasons in your explanation. Hint
An independently sourced check solution contains 2.00 mg Fe/L in the final solution. Our exercise acceptance window is 95–105% recovery. It checks the calibration in block A and again before the later block B.
qc <- read_csv("data/qc.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
qc_summary <- qc |>
  group_by(block) |>
  summarise(mean_absorbance = mean(absorbance),
            reference_mg_l = first(reference_mg_l), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(estimated_mg_l = (mean_absorbance - a) / b,
         recovery_percent = 100 * estimated_mg_l / reference_mg_l,
         qc_pass = recovery_percent >= 95 & recovery_percent <= 105)
qc_summary



Block A passes the exercise QC rule; the later block B fails.


A recovers about 99.6%. B recovers about 85.2%. Withhold P05 from B, even though its signal is inside the calibration range. Investigate, correct the problem, establish satisfactory calibration and QC, and remeasure the sample. Do not automatically divide results by 0.852: the cause of the failure is not established. A passing simple check also does not prove that every sample matrix is free from interference.
Now combine the two checks so unsupported estimates cannot appear as results:
results <- joined |>
  left_join(range_check, by = "preparation_id") |>
  left_join(qc_summary |> select(block, qc_pass), by = "block") |>
  mutate(reportable = in_range & qc_pass,
         final_mg_l = if_else(reportable,
                              (mean_absorbance - a) / b, NA_real_),
         original_mg_l = final_mg_l * final_ml / aliquot_ml)
results |> select(preparation_id, sample_id, original_mg_l, reportable)
write_csv(results, "output/student-concentrations.csv", na = "NA")
Missing values here mean withheld analytical estimates, not zero iron. Include the reason for withholding in your report.


R7. Extend the earlier course with uncertainty
Calculate P01 standard uncertainty and distinguish it from the helper’s approximate 95% final-solution interval. State the omitted sources. Hint
Repeated readings do not remove uncertainty in the calibration or in the preparation volumes. A simple concentration estimate also needs uncertainty from the fitted slope and intercept. NIST calibration guidance
Run the supplied helper for P01; you do not need to write a function:
source("R/inverse-calibration.R")
p01_readings <- readings |> filter(preparation_id == "P01")
u_p01 <- inverse_calibration(fit, p01_readings$absorbance)
u_p01
It returns the point estimate, an approximate standard uncertainty from response and calibration, and an approximate 95% interval for final concentration. For P01, these are about 2.3981 mg Fe/L, 0.00451 mg Fe/L, and 2.3886–2.4077 mg Fe/L respectively. These are different summaries: standard uncertainty is not a 95% half-width.
The helper assumes a correct linear model, independent normal response errors with constant variance, negligible calibration-concentration uncertainty, and the same reading variance for standards and unknowns. It uses a first-order approximation appropriate for this well-determined slope. It does not validate those assumptions for another dataset. Forward predict() intervals alone are not concentration intervals; the helper propagates through the inverse relation.
Add independent supplied volume uncertainties using the relation below. Here \(u\) denotes standard uncertainty:
\[u(c_{original})=\sqrt{(D u(c_{final}))^2+
\left(c_{original}\frac{u(V_{final})}{V_{final}}\right)^2+
\left(c_{original}\frac{u(V_{aliquot})}{V_{aliquot}}\right)^2}\]
p01 <- results |> filter(preparation_id == "P01")
D <- p01$final_ml / p01$aliquot_ml
u_original <- sqrt(
  (D * u_p01$u_cal_mg_l)^2 +
  (p01$original_mg_l * p01$u_final_ml / p01$final_ml)^2 +
  (p01$original_mg_l * p01$u_aliquot_ml / p01$aliquot_ml)^2)
u_original



Response and calibration dominate this illustrative uncertainty budget for P01.


One suitable statement is: P01 gave 11.991 mg Fe/L with a standard uncertainty of 0.028 mg Fe/L from the stated calibration, reading, and volume model. This is not a full method uncertainty or a 95% interval. The budget excludes sampling, matrix bias, incomplete recovery, and uncertain standard concentrations. Keep full precision for calculations and round only reported values.
P01 and P02 share a calibration and come from the same collected sample. Do not average their uncertainty estimates as though they were independent calibrations, or describe six readings as six water samples.


R8. Your report and transfer task
Produce the report and calculate the new preparation below. Explain its reporting conditions as well as its concentration. Hint

Render the supplied report.Rmd unchanged, then save an edited copy at the project root. Explain the absorber, wavelength, concentration basis, and assumed preparation chemistry.
Add the spectral, calibration, and residual plots with your interpretations.
Complete the ID join, range checks, and QC checks. Report P01, P02, and P04 separately and explain why P03 and P05 do not have reportable concentrations.
Add P01’s uncertainty calculation and state the omissions. Explain why the SD of its three absorbances alone is insufficient.
For a new preparation, a 2.00 mL aliquot was made up to 50.00 mL. Its three readings are 0.399, 0.401, and 0.400 in accepted block A. Estimate the original concentration. Compare its preparation factor with P01’s.
Restart R and render using rmarkdown::render("report.Rmd", output_dir = "reports") from the console. Keep the source, input data, CSV results, and HTML report together.







Numerical checks





P01 ≈ 11.99 mg Fe/L, P02 ≈ 12.10 mg Fe/L, P04 ≈ 27.00 mg Fe/L. P03 needs remeasurement; P05 is withheld after QC failure. For the new preparation, \(\bar A=0.400\), \(D=25\), and the original concentration is approximately 49.81 mg Fe/L. This is a point estimate, not a complete uncertainty statement.









Check your reasoning






Incomplete reduction? Less absorbing Fe(II) complex can give a low result.
Why not subtract the blank again? The supplied absorbances already use it as the reference. A further subtraction would change the measurement basis.
Why is a good line insufficient? Sample range, recovery, selectivity, preparation, and current QC still matter.
Does a QC failure identify its cause? No. It signals that results need to be withheld and the measurement process investigated.
Can more scans replace more samples? No. Wavelength positions and repeated readings are not independently collected waters.




Selected textbook reading: Harris and Lucy, topics on molecular absorption, spectrophotometers, calibration, and experimental uncertainty. Read by topic; the edition for the planned course remains to be confirmed.

title: Exercise: UV and visible absorption
text:
Hints






B1: invert the logarithm





Use \(A=-\log_{10}T\), then \(T=10^{-A}\). Doubling the exponent squares the transmittance; it does not subtract a fixed fraction.









B2: final before original





Rearrange the fitted response as \(c=(A-a)/b\). The preparation factor is final total volume divided by sample aliquot, with matching volume units.









B3: evidence gates are separate





An in-range response does not repair a failed independent QC condition.









B4: inspect the concentration unit





Use \(c=A/(\varepsilon l)\). A coefficient per mol/L requires concentration in mol/L; the empirical iron line instead uses mg elemental Fe/L.









E1: hold other optical effects fixed





In the stray-free model, doubled path doubles absorbance and squares transmittance. With an unchanged cell/wavelength calibration, interpret the candidate separately from the matching and range decisions.









E2: sensitivity versus concentration





The illustrative envelope has lower sensitivity at 450 nm. Compare the new response with standards recalibrated under the same wavelength and path.









E3: inspect only the standard rows





A response floor is nonlinear. Fit absorbance ~ concentration_mg_l only after filtering the export to record_type == "standard"; sample truth is not a calibration standard. The optional import in the solution is guarded so your ordinary R workflow still runs without a downloaded CSV.









R1: row meaning





A wavelength position within one scan is not an independently prepared solution. A spectral maximum improves response but does not prove chemical specificity.









R2: measured response direction





lm fits absorbance on known concentration. Look for curvature and changing spread before inverting; retaining an intercept does not establish the physical cause of an offset.









R3: key matching





left_join uses IDs, not row positions. Unique preparation keys avoid duplicated measurement rows; complete matches avoid losing the correct dilution volumes.









R4: return through the volume chain





P01’s mean absorbance is 0.480620. Use the fitted coefficients at full precision, then multiply by 50.00/10.00. Final volume includes reagents and solvent.









R5: old reading versus new evidence





P03’s signal exceeds the standard range. P04 has its own measurement and a new 5.00 mL aliquot; changing the number attached to P03 would not supply that evidence.









R6: retain the failure reason





if_else() leaves unsupported estimates as NA_real_. Block A and later B have different check evidence; failed B does not retrospectively invalidate A.









R7: identify the scale and coverage





The helper’s final-concentration standard uncertainty, its approximate 95% interval and the combined original-concentration standard uncertainty are three different summaries. Do not use one name for all of them.









R8: transfer the measured preparation





The new readings average 0.400. Its aliquot is 2.00 mL, not P01’s 10.00 mL; its factor is 50.00/2.00. Use accepted block A and the stated assay assumptions.

title: Exercise: UV and visible absorption
text:
Solutions






By hand and optical exploration





B1. \(A=-\log_{10}(0.50)=0.30103\). Doubling gives 0.60206, so \(T=10^{-0.60206}=\mathbf{0.25}\). This happens to equal half of 0.50, but the general relationship is squaring, not halving. Starting instead at 0.80 gives \(A=0.09691\) and doubled absorbance gives \(T=0.80^2=\mathbf{0.64}\), not 0.40.
B2. Final concentration is \((0.4806-0.004)/0.199=\mathbf{2.39497}\) mg Fe/L. The original-water factor is \(50.00/10.00=5\), giving 11.9749 mg Fe/L. The slightly rounded hand line differs from the later fitted data line; neither answer refers to mg complex/L.
B3. Withhold the affected later-block sample despite an in-range signal. Investigate, establish satisfactory calibration/checks, and remeasure. The 85.2% recovery does not identify the failure cause or establish a valid universal correction by division.
B4. \(c=0.600/(2000\times1.00)=\mathbf{3.00\times10^{-4}}\) mol/L. This is a separate supplied absorber example. The iron slope in L/mg Fe uses an elemental mass concentration; a molar absorptivity uses mol/L and a stated path. Conversion of the concentration basis is required before comparing their numerical values.
E1. At reset, input is 2.4 mg Fe/L. Doubling path doubles ideal absorbance from 0.47712 to 0.95424 and squares transmission. Recalibration at the selected path still returns 2.400 mg Fe/L. With recalibration off, the old 1 cm line gives a candidate 4.800 mg Fe/L: the demo withholds it because cell conditions differ and the candidate exceeds the prepared 0–4 mg/L range. A candidate is not made reportable merely because an algebraic inverse exists.
E2. Sensitivity and absorbance decrease; transmission increases. The matched stray-free calibration returns the same 2.400 mg Fe/L concentration in this noise-free model. It cannot establish real precision or selectivity at the new wavelength.
E3. Unabsorbed stray light creates a transmission floor. The underlying response bends down relative to Beer–Lambert even after fitting a straight line to the standards. A small departure might remain within the exercise’s 0.005-absorbance check; a larger one fails it. Passing that threshold is not a complete method validation. To reproduce exported standard residuals, save the CSV in output/uv-visible-demo.csv and optionally run:
demo_path <- "output/uv-visible-demo.csv"
if (file.exists(demo_path)) {
  demo <- read_csv(demo_path, show_col_types = FALSE)
  demo_standards <- demo |> filter(record_type == "standard")
  demo_fit <- lm(absorbance ~ concentration_mg_l, data = demo_standards)
  demo_standards <- demo_standards |> mutate(residual = residuals(demo_fit))
  ggplot(demo_standards, aes(concentration_mg_l, residual)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") + geom_point() +
    labs(x = "Prepared standard (mg Fe/L)", y = "Residual absorbance") +
    theme_minimal()
}









R1–R8: full analysis and reporting interpretation





R1. The standard has its illustrative maximum near 510 nm and the reagent blank is small. A strong local maximum supports sensitivity and reduces the first-order effect of a small wavelength-setting error relative to a steep flank. It does not show that the sample has no other absorbing component. Rows are positions in one spectral scan, not many independent standards.
R2. The fitted intercept is about 0.003873883, slope 0.198799368 L/mg Fe. Residuals are small without an obvious curved pattern in these simulated standards. Retain the intercept rather than force zero. The residual pattern neither identifies the offset’s cause nor establishes recovery/selectivity in an unknown sample matrix. Reversing the regression is a different fit.
R3. The key checks establish one preparation record per ID and a match for every measured preparation. left_join(..., by = "preparation_id") therefore attaches the correct aliquot, final volume and block despite reversed table order. P01/P02 are two preparations of W1, each with three repeated readings; they are not six separately collected waters.
R4. P01 mean absorbance is 0.480620. Inverting the fitted line gives 2.3981269 mg Fe/L final, then multiplying by five gives 11.9906346 mg Fe/L original. This uses total final volume, including all reagents and solvent.
R5. P03 is outside range and needs appropriate new measurement. P04 is a new 5.00 mL aliquot made to 50.00 mL, measured at mean absorbance 0.540610. Its factor is ten, giving 26.9988844 mg Fe/L original. It does not validate the old P03 reading by retroactive relabelling.
R6. Block A recovers 99.647% and passes the supplied 95–105% rule; later B recovers 85.176% and fails. P01, P02 and P04 are supported under the stated assumptions, at about 11.99, 12.10 and 27.00 mg Fe/L original. P03/P05 are withheld for range/QC respectively. Their NA concentrations are not zero analyte. A passing check still does not establish every sample’s matrix behaviour or original digestion recovery.
R7. P01 final-concentration standard uncertainty is 0.00450904 mg Fe/L; its approximate 95% interval is 2.388568–2.407686 mg Fe/L final under the helper’s independent normal, equal-variance response model, negligible standard- concentration uncertainty and well-determined positive slope. Scaling the standard uncertainty by dilution and combining the independent volume terms produces 0.0276962 mg Fe/L original. A suitable statement is 11.991 mg Fe/L with standard uncertainty 0.028 mg Fe/L under this limited model, not a 95% half-width. Sampling, matrix bias, incomplete native recovery and standard- concentration uncertainty remain omitted. Shared calibration means uncertainty from two preparations must not be averaged as though both calibrations were independent.
R8. The separate new preparation averages 0.400. Its factor is 25:
transfer_final_mg_l <- (mean(c(0.399, 0.401, 0.400)) - a) / b
transfer_original_mg_l <- transfer_final_mg_l * 50.00 / 2.00
transfer_original_mg_l
The point estimate is 49.81481 mg Fe/L original, conditional on the accepted block, matching chemistry and in-range new reading. Its own preparation uncertainties are not supplied, so the point answer does not establish a full uncertainty. The final report should retain raw files, preparation IDs, model, plots, withheld reasons and rendered HTML, and run again from a fresh R session.

title: Exercise: UV and visible absorption
text:
Where this leads
Matrix effects and recovery asks why a correct calibration in simple standards can fail in a sample. Use the practice quiz to distinguish absorber, concentration basis, dilution, QC and uncertainty before moving on.

title: Quiz: UV and visible absorption
text:
Answer before opening the hint or explanation.

Q1. What species absorbs, and what iron quantity is reported?






Hint





Separate the prepared complex from the original oxidation state.









Answer





The prepared Fe(II)–phenanthroline complex absorbs. With quantitative reduction and complex formation, the result describes elemental iron in supplied filtered water, not its original Fe(II) fraction.




Q2. Why does doubling absorbance not halve transmitted light?






Hint





Invert the logarithm.









Answer





\(T=10^{-A}\). Doubling absorbance squares transmittance. At \(A=0.30103\), \(T=0.50\); at \(A=0.60206\), \(T=0.25\).




Q3. Should already reagent-blank-referenced absorbances be blank-corrected again?






Hint





Read the measurement basis.









Answer





No. Another subtraction changes the stated basis. A whole-procedure method blank can investigate a different contamination question.




Q4. Why fit absorbance on prepared concentration?






Hint





Which variable is deliberately set?









Answer





Concentration is the controlled input and absorbance the response. Invert that fitted response relationship for the unknown; reverse regression is a different error model.




Q5. P04 uses 5.00 mL made up to 50.00 mL. What factor restores the original basis?






Hint





Final total volume divided by aliquot.









Answer





The factor is 10. The signal must belong to that newly measured preparation; editing a factor cannot rescue an old out-of-range reading.




Q6. A sample is in range but its block QC fails. Is it reportable?






Hint





Range and independent check answer different questions.









Answer





Withhold it, investigate the failure, establish satisfactory calibration and QC and remeasure. The QC recovery alone does not identify a valid correction.




Q7. P01 and P02 are two preparations from the same supplied water W1. Do three readings from each give six independently collected water samples?






Hint





Track the hierarchy.









Answer





No. They are repeated readings nested within two preparations of one supplied water. They share sample origin and calibration.




Q8. What does the stated uncertainty omit?






Hint





Ask what the mathematical model includes.









Answer





The example includes reading/calibration and supplied volume uncertainties under stated independence assumptions. Sampling, matrix bias, incomplete recovery and uncertain standard concentrations are excluded; it is not full method uncertainty.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
text:
About this lecture

Separate multiplicative response effects, additive interference and earlier analyte loss.
Calculate incremental recovery and a fixed-volume standard addition.
State which assumptions make the negative intercept meaningful.


The exercise begins with pen-and-paper tasks, then embeds the exploratory model and finishes in R using the existing course datasets. Keep each numerical result connected to its chemical quantity. All data and profiles are simulated; the demonstrations do not validate actual instruments or preparation methods.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
section: Why can a good external line give a low result?
text:
Why can a good external line give a low result?

The sample changes the response per unit analyte.

Introduce multiplicative matrix suppression. A correct fit in simple solvent is not evidence that sensitivity is unchanged in sample.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
text:
Separate multiplicative and additive effects

Changed sensitivity and unrelated background are different problems.

Standard addition can address some sensitivity differences; it does not automatically subtract an unknown interferent.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
text:
A spike tests incremental response

What should adding a known amount change?

The increase, after matched dilution and preparation, should reflect the supplied analyte increment under the method assumptions.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
section: Put all terms on the same volume basis
text:
Put all terms on the same volume basis

Both final flasks have the same sample fraction and total volume.

If volumes differ, raw concentration differences can mix dilution with recovery. Here added concentration is explicitly final-flask concentration.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
text:
Calculate the observed recovery

Estimate rises from 1.50 to 2.25 mg/L after adding 1.00 mg/L.

The incremental recovery is seventy-five percent. State that no universal acceptance window is supplied for all matrices.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
text:
Interpret 75% correctly

It is evidence about the added analyte from its addition point onward.

It does not prove that every native analyte molecule experiences exactly the same loss.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
section: A late addition misses early extraction losses
text:
A late addition misses early extraction losses

Which step did the spike not pass through?

A post-extraction spike cannot establish extraction recovery. Even a pre-extraction free spike may differ from native bound analyte.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
text:
Build a fixed-volume standard-addition series

Every flask: 10.00 mL sample made to 25.00 mL.

Vary standard addition, not the final matrix fraction. Added concentration is expressed in the final flask.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
section: Write the sample contribution in the final flask
text:
Write the sample contribution in the final flask

c_{native,final}=c_s V_s/V_f.

The original sample is diluted to forty percent of its original concentration. This contribution remains the same across flasks.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
text:
State the response model
y=b(c_sV_s/V_f+c_{added,final}).

Background has already been corrected. Sensitivity is assumed constant across flasks and equal for native and added analyte. The model, not the graph alone, enables inference.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
text:
Fit the familiar straight line

lm(blank_corrected_signal ~ spike_mg_l_final, data = additions)

Reuse lm. The new idea is the experimental design and chemical meaning of its intercept.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
text:
Read the slope

Matrix slope ≈ 0.1496, versus external ≈ 0.1998.

Units are signal units per mg/L. The sample suppresses response in the teaching model.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
text:
Read the intercept

Response at zero added analyte ≈ 0.3004.

Zero added analyte still leaves native analyte in every sample aliquot. This is not the same as a zero-analyte blank.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
text:
Locate the negative intercept

x_0=-a/b\approx-2.0080 mg/L.

It is a model-based extrapolation. No negative solution is prepared.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
section: Undo the dilution of the sample aliquot
text:
Undo the dilution of the sample aliquot

2.0080 × 25.00/10.00 = 5.020 mg/L original.

The magnitude of the intercept refers to the final flask. Omitting the volume correction leaves the wrong sample basis.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
text:
Compare external calibration

The external answer is about 3.761 mg/L original.

The lower matrix sensitivity explains a low external result under this model. The comparison is not proof of the same mechanism in all future samples.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
text:
Extrapolation requires its own justification

Why is this different from reporting an ordinary unknown beyond range?

The negative intercept follows a designed additive model with fixed sample fraction. It is still uncertain and sensitive to model failure. Ordinary high unknowns need new measurements.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
section: An additive interferent can survive standard addition
text:
An additive interferent can survive standard addition

A positive non-analyte signal can shift the intercept.

Even an excellent straight line can then overestimate native analyte. Background correction must be chemically appropriate.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
section: Changing final volume changes the design
text:
Changing final volume changes the design

Do not use a fixed-volume intercept formula without its fixed-volume conditions.

Different final volumes alter native concentration and matrix fraction. A suitable alternative calculation must account for them.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
section: Uncertainty belongs to the inferred intercept too
text:
Uncertainty belongs to the inferred intercept too

Slope, intercept, their covariance and volume factors contribute.

This core exercise reports a conditional point estimate. The response interval at zero added analyte is not automatically an interval for original concentration.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
section: Do not turn one recovery into a universal correction
text:
Do not turn one recovery into a universal correction

What evidence would support applying a correction to another sample?

Matrix consistency, spike/native equivalence, validated behaviour and correction uncertainty would be needed. A convenient ratio is insufficient.

title: Matrix effects and recovery
text:
Transfer the design

5.00 mL to 20.00 mL; y=0.240+0.120c_{added,final}.

Negative intercept is minus two mg/L; original concentration is eight mg/L. Require the dilution explanation.

By hand, embedded experiment and R tasks · Practice quiz.
Save the calculation and a chemical interpretation in your reproducible report.
Interactive experiment · Predict, change, explain.

Harris and Lucy reading: calibration and spectrophotometric applications. Source and dataset assumptions are linked in the student page. Keep longer coding in the practical, rather than reading a script aloud. Allow thinking time where the question warrants it; keep a shorter deck when that serves the explanation.

title: Exercise: elemental measurements and dry-mass reporting
text: Connect the atomic absorption/emission signal path to an elemental quantity, recognise spectral overlap, and calculate copper per original dry mass with correct dilution and method-blank bases. Explain why elemental detection does not establish original molecular identity or digestion recovery.

title: Exercise: elemental measurements and dry-mass reporting
text: Connect the atomic absorption/emission signal path to an elemental quantity, recognise spectral overlap, and calculate copper per original dry mass with correct dilution and method-blank bases. Explain why elemental detection does not establish original molecular identity or digestion recovery.

title: Exercise: elemental measurements and dry-mass reporting
text:
Background
Atomic absorption measures attenuation of suitable source light by free atoms. Optical emission measures light produced by an excited population. Atomisation and excitation change the sample; a copper amount does not identify the original copper-binding molecule or oxidation state. Flame AAS, graphite-furnace AAS and ICP-OES differ in introduction and atomisation/excitation conditions.
The supplied elemental case calibrates introduced-solution copper in mg/L from emission counts. A dry sample is digested to a known volume, then diluted again before measurement. The method blank is a separate digest measured without that further dilution. Undo the sample dilution before subtracting the blank on a common digest concentration basis. All data and spectra are simulated.

title: Exercise: elemental measurements and dry-mass reporting
text:
By hand
B1. Write the signal path for AAS and for ICP optical emission. Which uses an element-specific light source, and which observes light emitted after plasma excitation? State one kind of chemical information atomisation does not retain. Hint
B2. A 0.2500 g dry sample is made to 50.00 mL digest. Its twofold dilution measures 0.40189 mg/L copper. The undiluted method blank is 0.001992 mg/L. Calculate corrected digest concentration, copper amount and mg/kg dry mass. Hint
B3. A second sample uses 0.2000 g dry material made to 25.00 mL. A fivefold dilution measures 0.0800 mg/L; undiluted method blank is 0.0100 mg/L. Calculate the result and explain why the blank is not multiplied by five. Hint
B4. A dissolved independent check recovers 100%. Does this establish complete plant digestion? Could a sample-specific neighbouring line still bias the sample while the simple check passes? Hint

title: Exercise: elemental measurements and dry-mass reporting
text:
Explore
The spectral model uses Gaussian lines on an offset axis, not authentic copper identification spectra. The isolated comparison line is idealised to share the same calibrated sensitivity without interference. Its output is a diagnostic apparent result, not validated reporting permission.



E1. Keep interferer height fixed and increase its distance from the target. Predict how the response at zero offset and apparent mg/kg result change. Explain why the total spectrum matters. Hint
E2. With visible overlap, switch blank subtraction off and on. Does blank correction remove the sample-specific overlap? Distinguish the two sources of excess response. Hint
E3. Select the ideal isolated line, vary the method blank and compare correct versus omitted blank subtraction. Export a scenario. Which evidence would be needed before treating a real alternative line as equally reliable? Hint

title: Exercise: elemental measurements and dry-mass reporting
text:
In R
Run the complete workflow at the project root in a fresh R session. A raw instrument offset represented by the calibration intercept is different from contamination measured by the whole-procedure method blank.
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
standards <- read_csv("data/course/atomic-standards.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
fit <- lm(emission_counts ~ copper_mg_l, data = standards)
a <- unname(coef(fit)[1]); b <- unname(coef(fit)[2])
qc <- read_csv("data/course/atomic-qc.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(estimated_mg_l = (emission_counts - a) / b,
         recovery_percent = 100 * estimated_mg_l / reference_mg_l,
         qc_pass = recovery_percent >= recovery_lower &
                   recovery_percent <= recovery_upper)
digests <- read_csv("data/course/atomic-digests.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
blank_digest_mg_l <- (digests$emission_counts[digests$sample_id == "method_blank"] - a) / b
results <- digests |>
  mutate(candidate_measured_mg_l = (emission_counts - a) / b,
         in_range = candidate_measured_mg_l >= 0 & candidate_measured_mg_l <= 2,
         corrected_digest_mg_l = candidate_measured_mg_l * further_dilution - blank_digest_mg_l,
         copper_mg_kg = if_else(sample_id != "method_blank" & in_range & all(qc$qc_pass),
           corrected_digest_mg_l * (digest_ml / 1000) / (dry_mass_g / 1000), NA_real_))
ggplot(standards, aes(copper_mg_l, emission_counts)) + geom_point() +
  geom_abline(intercept = a, slope = b) +
  labs(x = "Copper in introduced solution (mg/L)", y = "Emission counts") +
  theme_minimal()
qc
results
write_csv(results, "output/atomic-methods-exercise.csv", na = "NA")
R1. Interpret the calibration basis and independent-check recoveries. Why are those checks not plant recovery validation? Hint
R2. Report A1 and A2 on the correct original dry-mass basis. Explain the method blank’s missing sample mass and why it has no mg/kg sample result. Hint
R3. List the main uncertainty and recovery evidence missing from these point estimates. Distinguish elemental copper from original copper species, and explain why a stable response is not proof of selectivity. Hint

title: Exercise: elemental measurements and dry-mass reporting
text:
Hints






B1: follow the photons





AAS transmits a source beam through free atoms. ICP-OES observes emitted light from an excited plasma population. Neither preserves molecular identity.









B2: make the bases agree





Multiply sample measured concentration by two, then subtract the undiluted blank. Use litres for digest volume and kilograms for original mass.









B3: the blank has its own history





The blank’s concentration already refers to undiluted digest. It did not undergo the sample’s later fivefold dilution.









B4: trace the check material





A dissolved reference bypasses the destruction and extraction of native plant material. It need not contain the sample’s interfering element or matrix.









E1: contribution at the selected wavelength





An interferer’s peak maximum is not the only place it contributes. Its tail can add signal at the target wavelength.









E2: two different backgrounds





The method blank models material introduced during preparation. The sample’s spectral neighbour is a separate contribution absent from that blank.









E3: an ideal alternative is not a free instrument correction





Compare to the known model truth, but remember a real alternative line needs its own interference/background evaluation and appropriate calibration.









R1: count the reference path





lm relates counts to copper in the introduced solution. The check does not recreate the original plant digestion.









R2: convert the denominator





One gram is \(10^{-3}\) kg. The blank is not a plant sample with zero or unknown true sample mass; it has no meaningful dry-mass denominator.









R3: distinguish a point estimate from validation





Consider sampling, native recovery, weighing, volumes, calibration, blank variation and spectral/matrix effects.

title: Exercise: elemental measurements and dry-mass reporting
text:
Solutions






Full worked solutions





B1. AAS: element-specific source → free-atom population → wavelength selection → transmitted-light detector. ICP-OES: sample aerosol → plasma atomisation/excitation → emission-wavelength separation → detector. Original molecular identity and oxidation-state distribution are not established by the resulting total elemental signal.
B2. Digest concentration is \(0.40189\times2-0.001992=0.801788\) mg/L. Copper amount is \(0.801788\times0.05000=0.0400894\) mg. Dividing by 0.0002500 kg gives 160.3576 mg/kg dry mass. The result differs slightly from the later full-precision R value because the hand inputs were rounded.
B3. Corrected digest is \(0.0800\times5-0.0100=0.3900\) mg/L. Amount is 0.009750 mg, and dividing by 0.0002000 kg gives 48.75 mg/kg dry mass. Multiplying the undiluted blank by five would invent a dilution it never had.
B4. No. A dissolved check can recover quantitatively while native plant copper remains incompletely recovered. A spectral neighbour present only in the sample can also bias a target signal while a simple check passes.
E1. At fixed peak height, moving the interferer away reduces its Gaussian tail at zero offset. Apparent introduced concentration and apparent dry-mass result approach the true contribution. Looking only at the selected count hides why it changed; the neighbouring spectrum gives relevant interference evidence.
E2. Blank subtraction removes the known digest blank on its own basis. It does not remove the sample-specific overlapping line. Both omitted blank correction and spectral overlap can bias high, but they require different chemical evidence and remedies.
E3. With ideal isolation and correct blank subtraction, the model always returns 160.00 mg/kg: native digest 0.800 mg/L × 0.05000 L / 0.0002500 kg. Omitting blank subtraction increases the result by blank mg/L × 200. The alternative line is assumed equal-sensitivity and interference-free here; real work requires appropriate calibration, background and spectral/matrix checks.
R1. The line maps emission response to mg Cu/L introduced solution over 0–2 mg/L. Checks recover about 100.37% and 100.77%, within the supplied 95–105% exercise rule. They do not establish native plant digestion, sample selectivity or a complete uncertainty budget.
R2. Full-precision results are 160.3587 and 300.4236 mg Cu/kg dry mass. The method blank has no original plant mass, so its mg/kg field is NA. It supplies a preparation background estimate rather than an elemental result for a hypothetical zero-mass plant.
R3. The point estimates assume quantitative digestion/transfer, appropriate calibration and selected-signal specificity. A complete evaluation would need sampling/recovery evidence and relevant uncertainties in mass, volume, calibration and blank response, including correlations where relevant. Stable counts show repeatability, not necessarily chemical specificity. Copper amount does not identify the original molecule or oxidation state.

title: Exercise: elemental measurements and dry-mass reporting
text:
Where this leads
Separation principles show another way to distinguish components before detection. The practice quiz checks signal paths, blank bases and the limits of an elemental claim.

title: Quiz: atomic measurements
text:
Try each question before opening its hint. Then explain the answer in chemical and measurement terms. Lecture · Exercise.

Q1. Which optical signal distinguishes AAS from ICP-OES?






Hint





Ask whether the useful photons come from a source lamp or the excited sample.









Answer





AAS measures attenuation of suitable source light by free atoms. ICP-OES measures light emitted after plasma excitation and separates its wavelengths. ICP-OES is not ICP-MS, which detects ions by mass-to-charge.




Q2. A 0.5000 g dry sample is made to 25.00 mL digest. A fourfold dilution measures 0.300 mg/L copper; the undiluted method blank is 0.020 mg/L. Calculate mg Cu/kg dry.






Hint





Undo the sample dilution before subtracting the undiluted digest blank.









Answer





Digest is \(0.300\times4-0.020=1.180\) mg/L. Amount is \(1.180\times0.02500=0.02950\) mg. Divide by 0.0005000 kg to obtain 59.0 mg Cu/kg dry mass.




Q3. For the preceding sample, an analyst instead computes \((0.300-0.020)\times4\) as corrected digest concentration. Why is it wrong?






Hint





Was the method blank diluted fourfold?









Answer





The blank was measured undiluted. Subtracting it before multiplying by four subtracts four times its digest contribution rather than once. This gives 1.120 instead of 1.180 mg/L and biases the dry-mass result low by 3.0 mg/kg.




Q4. Counts at a selected wavelength repeat very consistently, but another element has a nearby line. Does the small SD establish copper selectivity?






Hint





Repeatability and attribution of a signal are different questions.









Answer





No. A reproducible overlapping contribution can give precise but biased copper estimates. Spectral/background evidence, appropriate alternative lines or justified corrections are needed; a method blank cannot automatically remove a sample-specific neighbour.




Q5. A dissolved copper check recovers 100%. Does it establish quantitative recovery from native plant material?






Hint





Which preparation steps did the dissolved check bypass?









Answer





No. It does not recreate release from the plant matrix or establish digestion completeness. A suitable reference material or relevant recovery evidence must challenge the native preparation, with its own assumptions.




Q6. Does a dry-mass copper concentration identify its original copper-containing molecule or oxidation state?






Hint





Atomisation changes the material.









Answer





No. The elemental result does not preserve that chemical identity. A specific species claim needs a species-preserving preparation and suitable selective evidence. The concentration basis must still distinguish digest mg/L from original dry mg/kg.

title: Separation principles
text:
About this lecture
Separate a mixture before assigning a detector response to an analyte.

Connect phase exchange to retention.
Calculate retention factors and resolution with defined widths.
Decide what a chromatogram can support.


Begin with the analytical problem: a detector can respond to more than one substance. Separation can make the response more selective, but it is not a guarantee of identity or purity. The exercise begins with small hand calculations, then the demo, then R.

title: Separation principles
section: A column picture is not a chromatogram
text:
A column picture is not a chromatogram
This is a position snapshot inside a column. The less-retained band is nearer the outlet.


The figure shows two bands at one instant, not two peaks on a time axis. Ask which reaches a detector at the right-hand outlet first. Bands also spread during migration. All drawings here are concepts, not exact instrument engineering.

title: Separation principles
section: Repeated exchange sets the average migration speed
text:
Repeated exchange sets the average migration speed
Solute travels with the mobile phase and is delayed by stationary-phase residence.


Molecules repeatedly exchange between phases. More time in the stationary phase gives lower average speed under this simple equilibrium picture. Composition, stationary-phase chemistry and temperature can change relative retention.

title: Separation principles
text:
Now read a detector trace
The chromatogram records response versus elapsed time.
The dashed reference is the unretained transit time t_0=1.00 min.


One row in the supplied trace is a time position in one run, not an independent sample. The dashed marker is not an analyte peak. Distinguish within-run sampling density from the number of injected or collected samples.

title: Separation principles
text:
Subtract transit before describing retention
k=(t_R-t_0)/t_0. For A, (3.00-1.00)/1.00=2.00.
For B, k=3.00; relative selectivity is \alpha=k_B/k_A=1.50.


The factor is dimensionless because all times use minutes. Dividing retention time by t0 without the subtraction would give three for A, which includes transit. The definition refers to stated method conditions.

title: Separation principles
section: Area, height and amount are different quantities
text:
Area, height and amount are different quantities
A broader peak can be lower while retaining the same integrated area.
Area still needs an appropriate calibration to become an amount.


The simulated A and B areas stay at 100 and 150 response·min in all three runs. A larger detector response is not a universal count of molecules; response factors and detector selectivity matter.

title: Separation principles
text:
Resolution needs a defined width
R_s=2(t_{R2}-t_{R1})/(w_1+w_2) for baseline widths.
For this pair: 2(4.00-3.00)/(0.40+0.50)=2.222.


Ask students to identify which export column supplies the width. Half-height widths need a different coefficient. All time units must match. The formulas describe a peak model; they do not establish the chemical identity of the material.

title: Separation principles
text:
Changing spacing changes separation
The overlap run retains both component areas but has R_s=0.667.


In the model only the spacing changes. If the detector responds to both substances, a combined area is not a compound-specific amount. An apparent maximum at an expected retention time does not prove that the candidate peak is pure.

title: Separation principles
text:
Changing width also changes separation
The broad run keeps the original retention times but has R_s=0.909.


Now separate the cause from the previous example: the spacing is unchanged, but both bands are wider. Extra-column volume, injection conditions, dispersion and mass transfer can affect width in real methods.

title: Separation principles
section: An integration boundary is not new selectivity
text:
An integration boundary is not new selectivity
Drawing a split between maxima does not independently identify each contribution.


A constrained integration or deconvolution model can sometimes be justified, but the boundary alone is not evidence. Ask what new measurement would help: changed separation, an appropriate detector dimension, or a verified reference comparison.

title: Separation principles
section: Why a single threshold cannot prove purity
text:
Why a single threshold cannot prove purity
At fixed R_s, a much larger neighbouring component can contribute more to the target window.


Values around 1.5 are a useful reference for similar Gaussian peaks, not universal proof of adequate quantification. Relative amounts, tails, detector selectivity and the required error matter. The demo holds A area fixed while changing B’s area so the distinction is visible.

title: Separation principles
section: Efficiency and selectivity solve different problems
text:
Efficiency and selectivity solve different problems
For an ideal Gaussian, N=16(t_R/w_b)^2.
Narrower bands improve efficiency; changed interactions can alter selectivity.


Do not swap baseline and half-height formulas. A highly efficient column cannot always rescue an unsuitable relative interaction. Keep the chemical separation question ahead of collecting instrument metrics.

title: Separation principles
section: Velocity trades off different broadening mechanisms
text:
Velocity trades off different broadening mechanisms
Conceptual model: H=A+B/u+Cu.


At very low velocity diffusion has more time; at high velocity finite mass transfer can broaden bands. These dimensionless values illustrate the shape, not actual optimum settings. Pressure and analysis time also affect method choice.

title: Separation principles
section: Use familiar R operations for the new quantities
text:
Use familiar R operations for the new quantities
peaks |> mutate(k = (t_r_min - t0_min) / t0_min)
Keep run, compound and width definition attached to the calculation.

Students already know mutate and grouped summaries. The learning is retention and width meaning, not a new programming package. Explain why a time-series row is not an independent replicate. The exercise includes complete worked R code after the tasks.

title: Separation principles
text:
Predict before exploring
Double both baseline widths without changing retention times.
What happens to R_s, height and complete component area?


Resolution halves; each Gaussian height halves at fixed area, while the complete areas stay constant. Then ask about a selected finite integration window: it may include a greater fraction from a neighbour. Use the exercise’s embedded demo rather than a separate app page.

title: Separation principles
text:
Return to the analytical claim
Expected retention supports identity under matched conditions; it is not conclusive by itself.
Calibration, adequate separation and sample preparation must all support the reported amount.


Draw the distinction between identity and quantity one last time. An absent obvious shoulder is not absence of a coeluting compound. Read Harris and Lucy by analytical-separation topic; IUPAC definitions are linked in the exercise.

title: Separation principles
section: Next: choose the transport and detector
text:
Next: choose the transport and detector

GC and HPLC build on these same retention and width ideas.

Keep extended coding in the exercise. The deck is sized for its teaching argument rather than a slide-count quota. Use the hand questions and predictions for discussion where students need time.

title: Exercise: GC, HPLC and internal-standard reasoning
text: Choose a plausible chromatographic route for a chemical question, calibrate integrated peak areas, and explain which shared effects an internal standard can compensate. Calculate first by hand; use the embedded experiment to test the assumptions; then analyse the supplied caffeine data in R.

title: Exercise: GC, HPLC and internal-standard reasoning
text:
Background
GC transports a vapour in a carrier gas; HPLC transports solute in a liquid. Introduction, stability, stationary-phase interactions and detector selectivity all belong to the method. A headspace GC method can sample volatiles above a nonvolatile matrix. A UV chromatogram still requires an absorbing analyte and adequate separation at the selected wavelength.
For this simulated HPLC case, final caffeine standards span 0–40 mg/L. Every standard and sample has 10 mg/L internal standard. Supplied integrated areas give these retained-intercept relationships:
\[A_{caffeine}=3+50c,\qquad R=A_{caffeine}/A_{IS}=0.006+0.100c.\]
The fixed internal-standard concentration is part of this calibration design. An internal standard can track only effects it experiences appropriately. A late addition cannot establish earlier extraction recovery, and a ratio cannot repair coelution or analyte-only matrix changes.

title: Exercise: GC, HPLC and internal-standard reasoning
text:
By hand
B1. Two injections of the same preparation give caffeine/IS areas 753/500 and 603/400. Calculate final concentration using external area and area ratio. The original-to-final dilution factor is 10. Report both sets on the original basis. Hint
B2. A new accepted injection gives areas 903/600, still with 10 mg/L IS and dilution factor 5. Calculate the original caffeine concentration using the ratio model. Hint
B3. Compare a volatile solvent mixture with an aqueous mixture of nonvolatile heat-sensitive compounds. Give a plausible GC/LC starting choice, and one condition that could change your decision. Hint
B4. A standard is added after extraction. Both resolved peaks share the same injection-volume variation, but only native caffeine lost 40% during extraction. Which effect can the ratio compensate? What additional assumption is needed if the standard is instead added before extraction? Hint

title: Exercise: GC, HPLC and internal-standard reasoning
text:
Explore
Predict before changing a control. The experiment varies injection, recovery, standard-addition timing and analyte-only matrix response while keeping a known simulation truth of 150 mg/L original caffeine. Constant offsets prevent perfect cancellation even in the otherwise matched model.



E1. At default recovery and matrix response, change injection multiplier from 0.8 to 1.0 and 1.2. Compare external and ratio estimates. Explain the small remaining ratio change rather than claiming exact invariance.
E2. Set injection multiplier to 1.0 and recovery to 60%. Compare IS added after and before extraction. Which condition is assumed when the early standard compensates? Does the constant offset disappear?
E3. Reset. Change only analyte response to 0.8, then separately introduce a known coeluting area of 100. Explain why neither effect is removed by an unchanged IS response. Which candidate remains calculable but is withheld?






Solutions — E1–E3





E1. At injection 0.8, external original is 120 mg/L while ratio original is 150.15 mg/L. At 1.0 both are150. At 1.2 external is 180 and ratio about 149.90. The common multiplicative injection factor mostly cancels in the ratio, but the constant caffeine-area offset3 does not scale with injection.
E2. At unit injection and 60% recovery, a late IS gives ratio original 90 mg/L: it never experienced the earlier loss. The early IS is assumed to have exactly the same recovery; its ratio original is about 150.40 mg/L, near the150 truth. The residual0.40 comes from the nonmultiplicative offset. Native/spiked material may behave differently in a real extraction, so early timing alone is not proof of equivalent recovery.
E3. With analyte-only response0.8 at the default injection 0.8, the ratio candidate is 120.15 mg/L, not150. With coeluting area 100 instead and all other settings reset, the candidate is 170.15 mg/L. Both selected model failures cause the original-concentration claim to be withheld: the ratio cannot supply missing chemical equivalence or selectivity. The candidate curves remain diagnostic.

title: Exercise: GC, HPLC and internal-standard reasoning
text:
In R
Run from the extracted project root. The supplied flags represent separation and QC review for this scenario, not switches to set after viewing a desired answer. lm() uses the familiar response-on-concentration direction.
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
standards <- read_csv("data/course/hplc-standards.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
injections <- read_csv("data/course/hplc-injections.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
R1. Add area ratio to both tables. Fit external-area and ratio calibrations and calculate each injection’s final and original candidate concentration. Which two injections belong to the same preparation? Hint
R2. Require range, supplied resolution and QC to pass before exporting a reportable original result. Which two injections must be withheld, and why? Plot the repeated D1 estimates by calibration approach. Hint
R3. Export a demo curve and, if available, import it in R. Plot the external and ratio candidates against injection multiplier. Distinguish a curve position in a model sweep from an independent sample. Hint

title: Exercise: GC, HPLC and internal-standard reasoning
text:
Hints






Hint — B1 and B2





Invert each fitted relationship separately. Compute \(R\) before subtracting its intercept. Multiply final concentration by the original-to-final preparation factor only once.









Hint — B3





Ask how each analyte can enter the mobile phase and whether it survives the conditions. Matrix and detector requirements can change a plausible first choice.









Hint — B4





Trace the analyte and standard through extraction and injection separately. Earlier timing helps only if their behaviour through the relevant step is appropriately equivalent.









Hint — R1





Use mutate(area_ratio = caffeine_area / internal_standard_area). Fit the ratios with final caffeine as explanatory variable, keeping the intercept.









Hint — R2





Combine independent evidence with &. if_else() can assign NA_real_ to unsupported concentrations; preserve the reason and preparation ID as well.









Hint — R3





The CSV separates candidate_... columns from reported_original_mg_l. A blank reported value imports as missing, not zero caffeine.

title: Exercise: GC, HPLC and internal-standard reasoning
text:
Solutions






Solutions — B1–B4





B1. External final concentrations are \((753-3)/50=15.00\) and \((603-3)/50=12.00\) mg/L. Ratios are1.506 and 1.5075, giving15.000 and 15.015 mg/L final. Original results are150 and 120 mg/L externally, and 150.000 and 150.150 by ratio. Their near agreement reflects compensation for a shared injection effect, not independent sample replication.
B2. \(R=903/600=1.505\); \(c=(1.505-0.006)/0.100=14.99\) mg/L final; original is 74.95 mg/L. This assumes accepted selectivity, range and QC.
B3. GC is a plausible start for the volatile solvent mixture; LC for the nonvolatile heat-sensitive aqueous solutes. Solubility, thermal stability, headspace partitioning, matrix compatibility or detector response could refine that choice. Neither instrument is universally best.
B4. The ratio can track shared injection variation but not caffeine loss before the late IS addition. An early IS would need sufficiently equivalent recovery and response; freely added standard and native bound analyte need not behave identically.









Full worked R solutions — R1–R3





R1.
standards <- standards |>
  mutate(area_ratio = caffeine_area / internal_standard_area)
fit_external <- lm(caffeine_area ~ caffeine_mg_l, data = standards)
fit_ratio <- lm(area_ratio ~ caffeine_mg_l, data = standards)
injections <- injections |>
  mutate(area_ratio = caffeine_area / internal_standard_area,
         final_external_mg_l = (caffeine_area - coef(fit_external)[1]) /
                                coef(fit_external)[2],
         final_ratio_mg_l = (area_ratio - coef(fit_ratio)[1]) /
                             coef(fit_ratio)[2],
         candidate_external_original_mg_l = final_external_mg_l * dilution_factor,
         candidate_ratio_original_mg_l = final_ratio_mg_l * dilution_factor)
injections
The fits are area 3+50c and ratio 0.006+0.100c. I1 and I2 are repeated injections of D1. Their final ratio estimates 15.000 and 15.015 agree much better than their external estimates 15 and 12. They do not establish two independent original drinks.
R2.
results <- injections |>
  mutate(in_range = final_ratio_mg_l >= 0 & final_ratio_mg_l <= 40,
         reportable = in_range & resolved & qc_pass,
         original_mg_l = if_else(reportable,
                                candidate_ratio_original_mg_l, NA_real_),
         decision = case_when(!qc_pass ~ "withhold: QC failed",
                              !resolved ~ "withhold: coelution",
                              !in_range ~ "remeasure: outside range",
                              TRUE ~ "conditional result"))
write_csv(results, "output/hplc-decisions.csv", na = "NA")
comparison <- bind_rows(
  filter(results, preparation_id == "D1") |>
    transmute(injection_id, method = "External area", estimate = final_external_mg_l),
  filter(results, preparation_id == "D1") |>
    transmute(injection_id, method = "Area ratio", estimate = final_ratio_mg_l))
ggplot(comparison, aes(injection_id, estimate, colour = method, group = method)) +
  geom_point() + geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Repeated injection of D1", y = "Estimated final caffeine (mg/L)") +
  theme_minimal()
I3 is unresolved and I4 has failed QC. Both reportable concentration fields are missing even though an algebraic candidate can be calculated. No zero-caffeine claim follows from either failure.
R3. This optional block runs only after saving the exported file in data/:
if (file.exists("data/internal-standard-experiment.csv")) {
  demo <- read_csv("data/internal-standard-experiment.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
  ggplot(demo, aes(injection_multiplier, candidate_ratio_original_mg_l)) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 150, linetype = "dashed") +
    labs(x = "Injection amount multiplier", y = "Ratio candidate original caffeine (mg/L)") +
    theme_minimal()
}
Changing multiplier walks through a deterministic model sweep; its rows are not additional sampled drinks. The explanatory controls encode known simulation effects. A real instrument does not automatically know native recovery or a coeluting contribution from its area ratio alone.

title: Exercise: GC, HPLC and internal-standard reasoning
text:
Where this leads
The integration case adds independent calibration, preparation and QC records. Defend an original-sample result with the complete evidence chain, not merely a well-behaved ratio or a familiar peak.

title: Quiz: chromatographic choices and internal standards
text:
Try the short calculations and method decisions before opening hints and explained answers. Assume all quantities refer to the stated final solution unless another basis is specified.
Q1. Which is a plausible starting method for nonvolatile heat-sensitive solutes in water: conventional GC or HPLC?






Hint





Consider entry into the mobile phase and stability under the method conditions.









Answer





HPLC is a plausible start because it transports dissolved solute without requiring ordinary GC vaporisation conditions. Solubility, stability, matrix compatibility and detector response still need evaluation; this is not a universal preference for LC.




Q2. The line is area\(=3+50c\). A resolved accepted sample has area 1003 and preparation factor 10. Calculate original concentration.






Hint





Invert the response line before applying the preparation factor.









Answer





\(c_{final}=(1003-3)/50=20\) mg/L. Original concentration is 20×10=200 mg/L, conditional on range, accepted QC, identity and preparation assumptions.




Q3. The ratio model is \(R=0.006+0.100c\). Areas are903 and 500, matched IS concentration, and preparation factor 5. What is the original caffeine estimate?






Hint





Compute903/500 first, then invert the ratio relationship.









Answer





\(R=1.806\), so \(c=(1.806-0.006)/0.100=18.00\) mg/L final. Original estimate is 90.00 mg/L. This is a point estimate under the stated calibration and evidence.




Q4. The standards all contain10 mg/L internal standard, but the sample accidentally contains 20 mg/L. Can the original ratio-versus-analyte-concentration line be applied unchanged?






Hint





What fixed design condition made that simple line appropriate?









Answer





No. The internal-standard concentration is part of the calibration relation. A different concentration changes the expected ratio. Use a justified concentration-ratio model or prepare matching samples; do not silently apply the old intercept and slope.




Q5. A standard is added after extraction. Both peaks share injection variation, but only native analyte suffered extraction loss. Does the ratio remove both effects?






Hint





Trace which steps the standard experienced.









Answer





It can compensate a sufficiently shared injection factor, but not earlier native loss that the late standard never experienced. Early addition is helpful only with appropriate equivalent behaviour, which needs evidence.




Q6. A matrix component contributes to the integrated caffeine peak but not to the internal-standard peak. Will taking their ratio restore caffeine selectivity?






Hint





The numerator contains which chemical contributions?









Answer





No. The ratio still includes the interfering contribution. Better separation or justified additional selective evidence is needed before the combined area supports caffeine quantification. A precise ratio can still be biased.




Q7. Two injections of one prepared drink agree closely. What replication claim do they support?






Hint





Distinguish collected sample, preparation and injection.









Answer





They provide evidence about repeated injection/measurement under those conditions. They are not two independent preparations or two independently obtained drinks. Shared extraction and calibration effects remain shared.



Lecture · Exercise and embedded exploration

title: Choosing and defending a result
text:
About this lecture
Defend a caffeine concentration from sample record to conclusion.

Use a new calibration and independent QC.
Keep range, separation and preparation evidence attached.
State uncertainty and unresolved actions.


This is the integration case, not a new software framework. The exercise has a complete independent dataset. Its idealised standards do not imply zero measurement uncertainty.

title: Choosing and defending a result
section: Choose the method for the chemical quantity
text:
Choose the method for the chemical quantity
Element amount and molecular caffeine identity require different evidence.


An atomising elemental measurement cannot preserve the original molecule. An unseparated UV response can include other absorbers. A suitable separation supports compound-specific interpretation but still needs identification, calibration and checks.

title: Choosing and defending a result
section: Use this case’s calibration and range
text:
Use this case’s calibration and range
Area = 4 + 40 × caffeine concentration, valid over 0–30 mg/L final.


These are different coefficients from the previous HPLC example. Reusing a fit because the analyte has the same name is not calibration. The standards are rounded ideal teaching points; their zero residual does not establish zero real uncertainty.

title: Choosing and defending a result
section: Check independently before using the line
text:
Check independently before using the line
The 15.00 mg/L check recovers 100.67%.
It passes the supplied 95–105% exercise window.


The observed area 608 gives 15.1 mg/L. Passing this check supports response under its conditions; it does not prove recovery or selectivity in every beverage. The window is a supplied teaching criterion, not a universal validation rule.

title: Choosing and defending a result
text:
Preparation history is chemical evidence
C1 and C2 use 5.00 mL to 50.00 mL.
C3 is a new 2.00 mL aliquot of the same drink as C2.


A new smaller aliquot changes the measured solution and requires a new response. An old signal is not made valid by editing the dilution factor. Keep original sample ID and preparation ID separate.

title: Choosing and defending a result
text:
C1 supports a conditional amount
Area604 → 15 mg/L final → 150 mg/L drink A.


The preparation factor is ten. Range, supplied resolution evidence and independent QC all pass. This remains conditional on the scenario identity and preparation assumptions.

title: Choosing and defending a result
text:
C2 is an out-of-range candidate
Area1604 implies a candidate 40 mg/L final.
Do not report that extrapolated concentration.


Algebra can return a number outside a validated range. Keep it diagnostic and withhold the reported estimate. The needed action is an appropriate new dilution and measurement, not a cosmetically altered table.

title: Choosing and defending a result
text:
C3 supplies new evidence
Area644 → 16 mg/L final.
Factor25 gives 400 mg/L drink B.


This valid new preparation does not retroactively make C2 a valid extrapolation. Explain why the final concentration decreases but the returned original concentration is higher than C1’s.

title: Choosing and defending a result
text:
C4 fails a different requirement
The area is inside range, but an unresolved component contributes.
Withhold the caffeine amount.


A ratio, perfect fit or repeated injection cannot by itself recover selectivity. Better separation or justified selective evidence is needed. The source final-case C4 signal is a supplied record; the interactive model is a separately defined exploration.

title: Choosing and defending a result
text:
Export reasons with the values
Withheld estimates are not zero concentrations.
Keep sample ID, preparation ID, factor and decision in the same table.


A reader should be able to audit an accepted result and understand an absent one. Missing values without explanations discard evidence; replacing them with zero creates a false chemical claim.

title: Choosing and defending a result
section: Read uncertainty on its stated scale
text:
Read uncertainty on its stated scale
C1: standard uncertainty 1.5 mg/L original.
C3: 4.0 mg/L original from the supplied final uncertainty.


The case supplies final standard uncertainties .15 and .16 mg/L; scale by ten and twenty-five. These are not ninety-five percent intervals and exclude volumes, sampling and recovery. The demo separately uses .15 for each new ideal preparation, so its two-millilitre result has3.75, not4.0.

title: Choosing and defending a result
section: A conditional budget is not full method validation
text:
A conditional budget is not full method validation
Ideal calibration points cannot prove zero uncertainty.
What evidence is missing for the intended use?


Ask for specific missing contributions: standard preparation, volumes, sampling, matrix recovery, identity and selection. State what the supplied budget includes and omits instead of appending an unexplained plus/minus value.

title: Choosing and defending a result
text:
Agreement is not association
Both methods track concentration; their differences tell different stories.


A high correlation can coexist with a large systematic discrepancy. Here nonspecific UV differs increasingly from the reference while HPLC differences are smaller. Reference uncertainty and required performance still matter.

title: Choosing and defending a result
section: A pattern motivates investigation; it does not prove cause
text:
A pattern motivates investigation; it does not prove cause
The UV discrepancy may motivate a matrix or selectivity study.


Do not conclude the chemical mechanism solely from the difference plot. The simulated data encode a bias pattern, not independent proof that a particular interferent caused it.

title: Choosing and defending a result
text:
What mass spectrometry can add
Ion source → mass analyser → detector.
The signal describes ions by mass-to-charge, not neutral mass directly.


This is a concise identity-evidence overview. It does not introduce a new advanced analysis workflow. Ionisation conditions determine which protonated, deprotonated, adducted or fragmented ions may appear.

title: Choosing and defending a result
section: Interpret a plausible caffeine ion carefully
